BABY. , Where did you come from, baby dear? I Out of the Everywhere into here. Where did you get those eyes so blue? Out of the sky as I came through_ : What makes the light in them sparkle and spin? Some of the starry spikes left in. • ' Where did you et that little tear? I found it waiting when I got here. ' What makes your forehead so smooth and high? A soft hand stroked it as I went by. ! What makes your cheek like a warm white rose? ' I saw something better than anyone knows. f Whence that three-cornered smile of bliss? Three angels gave me at once a kiss. f• Where did you get this pearly ear? God spoke, and it came out to hear. , Where did you get those arms and hands? • Love made itself into bonds and bands. • Feet, whence did you come, you darling things? From the same box as the cherub's wings. • How did they all just come to you? God thought about me, and so I grew. But how did you come to us, you dear? God thought about you, and so I am here. .—George Macdonald, from Sunday Magazine. -- A SHEPHERD'S CONSOLATION. " Non semper imbres."—Hor., Car. IL, 9. It's no' aye rainin on the misty Achils ; It's no' aye white wi' winter on Nigour ; The winds are no' sae mony sorrowing Rachels • That grieve, and o' their grief will not gie owre. Dark are Benarty's slopes, an' the steep Lomon' ' Flirts a lang, shadow on the wetter plain; But fair Lochleven's no' for ever gloomin', An' Devon's no' aye dark wi' Lammas rain. • The birks tho' bare, an' the sune-naked ashes Not always widowed of their leaves appear.; The oaks cry oot beneath November's lashes, But not for all the months that mak' the year. • Comes round a time, comes round at last tho' creepin', And green and glad again stand bus an' tree; E'en tender gowans thro' the young gress peepin', Rise in their weakness an' ower-rin the lea. Thus Nature sorrows, and forgets her sorrow; And Reason soberly approves her way: Why should we shut oor een against to-morrow, Because our sky was clouded yesterday? Dear Adie! for we've lang kent ane anither Tentin' our flocks upon the self-same hill, And if I speak as brither should to brither, Yell neither turn awa' nor tak' it ill,— It's now three years since little Adie left us; He was to every ane that kent him dear; Adam! it was the will of God bereft us, Called him awa', and left the lave o's here. • Three years ye've sorrowed for the little laddie, It clouds your broo, I hear it when ye speak. And thrice I've seen when ithers sawna, Adie, The suddetr tear upon your wasted cheek. Yenurse your sorrow in the cheerfu' morning, Ye nurse it, too, at unavailing eve; Our rustic gatherings with a silent scorning, ' And all our rural sports and joys ye leave. Sorrow is sacred, but this sair insistance This lang refusal to Heaven's will to Coo, Consider, Adie! is't a wise resistance? You'll go to him, he canna' come to you. And since you go to meet him, go not sadly, For the short half of life that yet remains; You love your son—go then to meet him gladly On that appointed day which Heaven ordains. —Hugh Haliburton, in Good Words.

From this statement it would aopear that inequality of assessment eNisted between the different townships and that the present aierage gross a.sessment in the Union is 6d per head of accommodation, and 9101 per head on average Wen- dance, It had been the custom of that committee to assess all elementary schools nominally, but it would be well that a definite system should be decided upon that the assess- ments, although nominal, should be even in the different townships. It would be well that the committee should de- cide upon a fixed sum per head on the accommodation, as being an unymying quantity from year to year, and as he had no reason to suppose it was the desire of the commit- , tee to raise the total assessment the amount might be fixed at 6d per head for the gross, subject to 15 per cent reduc- tion for rateable value. In some cases the assessment on accommodation, and not on 'attendance, might work a little unsatisfactorily, but these cases could be made the subject of appeal, but on the other hand, it the assessment b 3 fixed on the average attendance it would give considerable trouble to the overseers and also give rise to disputes. With regard to school houses he was of opinion they should be assessed at their value as houses, without connection with the schools, that is at the amount they would let for.

div.head: PRFSCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: PRFSCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The fortnightly meeting of the Present Board of aim• dians was held at the Union Workhouse, Whiston, on Thursday afternoon. when there were present : Mr J Fisher (chairman), Revs T Chambers and Dean Finegan, Measrs J Burchall, W Swift, J Buckley, .1 Ranson, C B Johnson, ' E Syder, R A Graves, P Longton Leatherbarrew, J Ken- wright, J W Wareinz. and S H dartley (clerk). RILIEF: INCREASED VAGRANCY. The Workhouse Master retrrted there were 477 inmates of the house this week,. 475 last week, and 451 in the corresponding period last year. During the week 104 vagrants had been relieved against 69 in the corresponding week last vear. In reply to Mr P Dongton, the Chairman said be thought the harvest time would account for the increase in the number of vagrants.

THE NEW RAINHILL ASYLUM.—The Clerk read a letter from the County Authorities stating that as the increased accommcdttion at Ralohill Asylum had been specially pro- vided for the requirements of the West Der by Hundred the General Finance Committee hoped the Board would see the desirability of making arrangements to send all lunatics from the union to that asylum. The Clerk intimated that he had written that the Guardians bat already anticipated the action of the County committee, and the Board would be pleased to know if the Rainhill charges had been reduced to the minimum amount. He had not yet received a reply. Wongworrsn BOILERS.—The Clerk read a report from the Boiler Insurance and Steam Power Co., Manchester, that one of their inspectors bad inspected boiler No. lat the Workhouse externally and internally. No defects were ob- served, and the boiler was reported to be Its a generally satisfactory condition. Tern Sr. HELENS RELIEVING OFFICE3.—The Clerk read a letter from Mr. C. M. Stuart, relieving officer at St. Helens, stating that the tenants were giving up possession of toe premises adjoining the offices, and increased accommodation was much needed. Mrs. Wilcock would make the desired alteration if the Guardians would take the premises for a term. It was stated that the premises had been used for the storage of furniture, and was situated near the railway station.—The Chairman asked if it was de- sirable they should have more accommodation.— Mr. Leatherbarrow said they were already paying from £25 to £3O a year for the present offices.—Mr. Buckley said if in- creased accommodation was provided the Relief Committee could meet there.—Mr. Wireing moved that the matter be referred to the Guardians for the townships of Parr, Sutton, Eccleston, and Windle —The Rev. Dean Finegan seconded the motion, which was adopted. , THE ESTIMATE —The Clerk submitted the estimates for the half-year ending March, 1838, as follows :—Mainten- ance £2500, children in schools £1,700, out relief £4,500, lunatics in asylums £2,600, instalment of loan £4BO, interest on loan £6OO, salaries of union officers £1,450, salaries of assistant overseers £750, workhouse officers' rations £250, Asse.ssatent Committee's expenses £lOO, school fees (non- paupeis) £5OO, vaccination expenses £290, registration ex- penses £220, esteelishment ch trees, workhouse, &c. £l.OOO, county rate £6o6o—total £23,000 • add 10 per cent for contingencies, £2,3oo—total £25,360. The total amount expended in the last half-year was £21,9.02. The Clerk stated there was a small reduction of about £44o.—The estimate was approved. HOLIDAYS —Mr. Tracey, relieving officer for Widnes was granted ten days holiday. IRE ALLEGED CASE OF HYDROPHOBTA.—The Clerk re- ported that with respect to the man Hancox, who was bit- ten by a dog, he and Mr. Leyland, veterinary surgeon, Prescot, with the master of the Workhouse, proceeded to Bold and saw the dog, and Mr. Leyland unhesitatingly pro- nounced the dog to he in a good state of health. He (the clerk) saw Dr. Hall en the following day, and Dr. Hall said he found the man in the Workhouse and be did not con- sider it any part of his duty to make inquiries outside the house. Other persons had been bitten by the dog, but he (the clerk) did not think there was any blame at- taching te the owner.—ln reply to a question, Vatt • Clerk sehled that . tbe man Hancox was still in the Workhouse, and was quite cheerful and happy.—The ser. Dean Finegan did not think Dr. Hall's explanation satisfactory, because at the last meeting Dr. Hall left them in the position of either incurring the risk of lotting the man die frem hydrophobia, or incurring a great expense in sending him to M. Pasteur, at Paris, as the doctor recommended.—Mr. Waieing abeerved that Dr. Hall had said that the man Hancox was a fit subject for M. Pasteur, without giving any reason, acd it was clearly de- monetrated that it was no case for M. P,,asteur. It might be quite right as Dr. Hall says that he ehould not go out of the house, but he might to cause inquiries to be made be- fore placing the Guardians in the position he had done.—The Rev. T. Chambers thought the medical officer was wrong in saying it was no part of his duty to see whether the dog was suffering rpm rabies or not.—The Rev. Dean Finegan was not at all satisfied with the manner in which Dr. Hall had treated the Board.—The Chairman asked if Dr. Hall should be called before the Board.—After some discussion the Rey. T. Chambers moved that the Clerk write to Dr. Hall asking him for another expression of opinion on the matter, and Mr. Johnson seconded the motion.—Mr. Ware-

ing moved an amendment that Dr. Hall be adred to attend the next Board meeting, and the Rev. Dean Finegan seconded.—On the amendment being nut to the vote six votpd in its favour and six against. The Chairman gave his casting vote in favour of the amendment, which was declared carried. This concluded the business.

div.head: SARAH BERNFIARDT'S IMMENSE RECEIPTS AND PATTI'S PERIL
div.p: SARAH BERNFIARDT'S IMMENSE RECEIPTS AND PATTI'S PERIL

Sarah Bernbardt's receipts, for her late tour in South America, are the largest ever taken by any dramatic artiste. But the reckless Sarah scarcely ever has a franc to spare ! Patti has also achieved great success, and a very large amount of money, in Mexico and South America, but came vary near being the victim of a dynimiter who attempted to throw an explosive bomb at her while she was singing at the Grand Opera House in San Francisco, California. She was called again and again in front of the curtain when, as she was finally retiring, a man in the gallery suddenly rose, picked up a bomb from under the seat, and raising it in the air, was about to throw it, when it exploded in his hand, shattering his arm and face, and inflicting other injuries. Had the man not placed himself under the protection of a policeman, who met him as he was rushing down stairs, he would have been torn in pieces by the in- furiated people. Patti displayed great coolness and pres- ence of mind, and succeeded in restoring quiet by singing " Home, Sweet Home."

Poor Patti! It is a wonder she was not killed by the nervous shock, or that she did not faint, or that her hair did not turn gray through fright. Think of Patti with gray hair! A beautiful head of hair is the crowning glory of woman, and its loss is her greatest misfortune—a mis- fortune which may be prevented by the use of that famous hair restorer and dressing, known as Mrs. S. A. Allen's World's Hair Restorer, which will prevent baldness and restore gray hair to its nataral color, strength and gloss. It can be had at any chemist's or perfumer's shop in the civilized world.

The question' "Does getting drunk ever advance one's happiness?" would seem to be put to rest by the Irishman who went courting when drunk, and when asked what pleasure be found in whisky, replied, "Oh, Nelly, it's a trate entirely to see two of your swate purty face instead of one."

CHAPTER XIV. SAVED. _ She the s.triour and he the eaved,—bliss born of the very smaller-place. —lirau-ning.

Dermot Grady and his companions passed out of the barn. Hyacinth listened till they had crossed the barn- yard, and were out of hearing. Then she glided out from her shelter, and creeping to the paling, looked through. She could just catch a glimpse of the black figures descending the,slope that led to the Curramore- road. The way she must take was half a mile longer. Therwere walking quickly but would not be likely to run. She must ran the whole way ; and she was as 'Set as a young antelope. She felt as if the strength and fleetness of twenty such elastic frames as hers were In her to-night. She was risking far more thaii life now,—nay, life she: risked, her good name she was flinging down to save a man'a life. She must be alone at Curramore with Vincent Lorraine. What of that ? What if all Ireland cried shame on her? She would be acquitted before Heaven, and in his eves who loved her. . Her way lay through long fields, over a wide strip of bog, along an imperfectly made road, and so out unto the moorland immediately surrounding Curramore. She started off like an arrow from a bow, running at a ! pace which, swift of foot as she was, astonished her- self. She seemed to fly. Well as she knew the road, she would not have run like this over the uneven ground, on a dark night, at any ordinary time; but now she had no fear of a stumble, and she did not stumble once; nor, till she had run more than two miles, did she slacken to take breath. Through the dark fields she went, and hedge and tree fleeted past like black phantoms; and as she ran, from the horizon broke forth a sullen mutter of thunder. She had slackened a little then—only a little—to take breath, but at that sound of thunder, her cheek, flushed with the rapid motion, blanched to a deadly hue. What if the men, fearing a sudden downpour of rain," hurried, forwards, and retched Curramore before her? The horrible fear urged her to madness; she fled on with a new energy. She was not far now—only a mile—one little mile;' there were'‘the three trees that grew together, and the white gate thitt led into Dan Murphy's corn field. flit had been light enough' she could &ye seen the towers of Curramore. What if Lorraine were out, and Margaret did not hear the bell, or would net come to the gate? . Away with such fears! Heayen was with her—helping her on—she could run miles—count- less thiles like this—it seethed hardly Seth :minutes ago- that she ha,il,left Grady's farm. - Now the moorland, and now she could just discern the black walls of Carramore looming through the darkness. Hark! another peal of thunder, louder and nearer! On, on, still on—over hillock and hollow ; and now she is .close, Is ',Lorraine within? She can see no light, but then the library window does not face her. Her heart grows -sick within her; for he may be absent; and the men would watch for his return, and shoot him down as he rode up to the gate, Are they there? No, no; they could not have come up yet, - they must be fully a mile behind. She sprang forward to the gate and pulled the bell with a force that would have 'woken a thousand echoes if the bell Within hid been a noisy one; still the heard it ring, and pulled again, listening with her heart-beats almost suffocating her—listening for a step within—for any sound of the approaching murderers; but they might be quite close, and she neither see nor hear them, between the dark- ness and the..soft turf. A bolt shot—a_ door opened—a hurried, shuffling step—lt pauses—a shrill voice cries --" Who's there widout ?" - ' " Hyatinth Desmond—open, for the love of God!" "Holy Vargin !" A heavy bolt driven back—oh, Heaven, how long the 'woman seemed in doing it !--4-a: key turned, and as Margaret began to open-the great gate, Hyacinth pushed it further, glided in, and with frantic haste, (psi each , strength as ,she had never shown before drove home the massive bolts, and tumid the key, and, linokud- across the two great chains. ; "Is he withrri—is Vincent Lorraine in? answer me?" For Margaret was struck dumb, though she had an instant idea of some grave ,peril. "Yes, shure be's in," she said, "Blessed Vargin! " "You speak tinthlb-sald Hyacinth; grasping the old woman's arm like a vice—" he.is in?" "Shure, miss - "Oh, thy life ! " the girl grasped out. " Saved ! Hush I'no queitionscome with met " She almost dragged the old woman across the court- yard, through the postern, into the kitchen, and shut and burred the postern in, the same excited manner as she had fastened up the gate, but yet with a kind of suppressed fire, as if she were assessed by some power that was 'whirling' her onwards, and whose behests rather than her own will she obeyed. Where is Viticent Lorraine she said, panting for breath, her dark eyes wild and glittering. 'I -n the library, miss, shure. Oh, what's the matter —what's happened ?" cried Margaret, trembling like a leaf. _ _

" fist ! they are coming to murder him; don't go to the gate again for your life—for his-----" A quick step in the passage—his step—the door was thing open, and Vincent Lorraine came in. "Great God! Iflyacinth

_ With a cry he never forgot, the girl sprang forwards to his breast, clinging_to him, as he locked his arms about her, like one distracted, utterly unable to speak, even to weep, but not fainting; no, the, strain was not over yet; though wild joy had crowned the awful an- guish; though she was held to her lover's heart, folded in his embrace of deathless love, though his warm lips pressed her broiv, and his soft voice, quivering with the agony that filled him, divining at least something of the truth, whispered soothingly. .But she strag- gled for breath, muttering brokenly, "You are saved— saved—l will—hush !" she paused, listening. Lorraine signed to Margaret to bring some water, but when she, came near with the glass. Hyacinth shook her head. "No, no, it will choke me." "Your lips are parched, Hyacinth. Try to drink a little, for my sake," Lorraine said. She obeyed at once; and after a moment spoke more collectedly. "They are coming here to-night to murder you—they must be close now. I heard them plan it all. I ran all the way from Grady's farm!" 'Hyacinth ! oh, my God, to save me, to save my worthless life r Ho stopped—he could not speak more; he wrapped the slender form closer and closer to him, and bowed his head on hers. That '.she should do this for him, whom perhaps she did not yet love; run such deadly risk—sacrifice her fair name—it was more than he could bear; but the girl said passionately—" If I had never seen you I must have tried to save von—and— and—" She had lifted her face, but hid it again, flushing crimson; and added hurriejlly—" Let me tell you—they will be here in a few minutes. I knew there was mischief plotting, and this evening I was at Grady's, and found out there was to be some meeting there; so when I left I stole round to the barn,— where I thought they would -meet—and hid behind some stacks of corn—no, hear me calmly, there was no real danger—" "No danger I" said Lorraine, hoarsely, "you were playing with your life !—Go on, my heart—l will be calm I" "I waited there," the girl went on, "till near eleven —about two . hours, I think, and then Grady, and Creagh, and Regan, and 'Kelly came in with a little boy, and two other men, Icho I Wl* are Dennis Maguire and Shemns Corrigan. But it was too dark to see them, and they had no light. And Grady said that the boy was to ring—the men hiding near—and; when Margaret came, he was to say he must see you; ! —she would not have any fear of a boy, and would ! open to let him in; and then the others would rush up, i and Margaret was to be gagged." (" Och I Holy Var. I gin I" here cried. Margaret, flinging up her hands. Hya-.! cinth went on not heeding her)—" And Grady would put on Margaret's list slippers, and go to the library,, and you would suspect nothing, and then he could shoot you." She stopped a moment. Lorraifie Wati white to the lips with the wild emotions that surged, within him, and his dark eyes glowed like fire. No word did he speak, but laid a trembling hand on that girl's soft curls; and she half smiled, and continnedk "When they had gone out to come here, I stole out., and ran round by the field road; it is half a mile fun. tber, I could not go their way, you know; and when. the thunder eame I thought they might hurry on and get here first, or that you were out, or Maagaret would not answer the bell."—She broke down now, and bowed ! her bead on her lover's breast, shuddering, and sobbing convulsiyely, but striving to control her agitation ; and, ah,! with what wondrous tenderness the man soothect ; her, putting an iron curb on his own emotion for he dear sake. , .

Th' noise he med wur like th' roor of a " buzzer," When roused fro his afternoon's nap, Bud lately he's changed otogether To a different sooart ov a chap. There have been heavy thunderstorms and rainfall in various parts of the country since Saturday last. ' Rain began to fall in the eastern parts of Lancashire on FridaT afternoon, and continued with little intermission until Saturday morning. On the evening of Saturday.there were thunderstorms on the western coast, accompanied by heavy falls of hail and rain. Fortunately.no serious damage was done. The storms were local. On Sunday there were thunderstorms in Preston and Bolton,one per- son being killed in the lattrer borough. Since then heavy showers fell at intervals. The rain has been welcomed by • both town and country people, who alike have suffered from the•cirought. -There is now'no fear of water famine In many districts, for the fl•Nwnpour has been the most enpious that has been experienced this season.. The fields and vegetation generally have been considerably refreshed by the fall, which it is hoped will continue for few days longer. - ,About six p.m. on Sunday, a severe thunderstorm passed over Buxton. At Dove lioles a house was de- molished by lightning, and six persons were struck by tho electric fluid. One, William Boothby, aged • 14, was - instantly killed. The others, who were stunned, and lie in a precarious.condition, are :—Mary Ellen Boothby, 20; Joseph Boothby, 13; Sarah Ann Boothby, 10; --Joseph Boothby, the father, and his wife. The boy who was killed was badly burnt on the body. A man named Lomas, a neighbour, was also stunned. There has been a heavy rainfall all over Cheshire, but, notwithstanding the recent rains, the rivers and brooks are lower than-within living memory. Rain began to fall in North-east Lancashire on Friday afternoon, and continued with little intermission until Saturday morn- ing. The downfall was the most copious that has been experieneed during the present season. The land, however, has swallowed it all up, and much more rain is needed to* enable the mills and workshops to resume work, '

When the storm was at its height on Sunday afternoon several houses situated in Back Queen-street, off Deans- gate, Bolton, were struck by lightning and partially ' wrecked. - A woman named Mary Joyce was killed, another woman named O'Toole was rendered insensible for a time, and two men, named Murphy and Edwards, were thrown down and injured. It was at first thought the houses had caught fire, and the fire brigade was sent for. About the same time a farm at Heaton, near Bolton, occupied by Mr. Thomas Pendlebury, was struck and set on fire, and before the tames were extinguished damage was done to buildings land stock to the extent of £l,OOO. A large Dumber of poultry and two cows were struck by the lightning and killed. trees in the neighbourhood wrecked, and over 50 P Wig of lay destroye-d. The heavy rainfall has done ..iletnothing towards replenishing the reservoirs in the dis- trict, which had got low in consequence of the continued drought "ELECTORAL FACTS OF 1887."

div.head: ARTICLE BY M. GLADSTONE.
div.p: ARTICLE BY M. GLADSTONE.

The forthcoming -number of the Nineteenth Century contains an article by Mr. Gladstone on the subject of " Electoral Facts of 1887." Mr. Gladstone says that political meteorology does not offer a field for the loftiest or most arduous exercise of thomfht, but yet it has both its interest and its justification. A rapid view may sug- gest that we have become involved in the instability which has often been the reproach of popular Govern- ments. After the accession of the House of Hanover, and again before the first Reform Act, Whigs and Tories respectively had each a lease of power for half a century. But stability such as that no one wishes to recall. After the Act of 1632 it took nine years to produce a Conserva- tive majority, and sixteen more years elapsed before the numericial superiority of professing Liberals was restored. We then passed through seventeen years, and in 1874 I saw the second Tory majority. Mr. Gladstone compares the period referred to with , that which took place after household suffrage came into , partial operation. The election of 1868 gave a Liberal ' majority of 110, which in 1874 was converted into a minority of 48. This was summarily converted in 1880 into a majority nearly the same as that of 1868. On the dissolutiomof 1885 the last and greatest enlargement of the franchise took effect. The Irish Nationalists fought in close accord with the Tory party. The Liberals, who had had a majority of 50 over their combined forces, were reduced to an exact moiety of the House, enlarged from 658 to 670. That election gave them a majority of 86 over the Tories; but when the Par- liament was again dissolved in 1886, while the entire nominal strength of the Liberal body was reduced to about 270, nearly 75 of these soon proved to be, in fact, for present purposes a portion of the Tory phalanx. The , united forces of the Government were thus raised to 390. The House was composed of four minorities, the largest being the Tory contingent, which reached 315'0r 316, 'whilst the Liberals in Opposition sank to 195, the lowest point to which either of the two great parties had declined since the Reform Act, with the exception of Sir Robert Peel's following in 1832. We had thus in eighteen years had five Parliaments returned wholly or partially by household suffrage, and every one of them had differed essentially in political complexion. Turning to recent elections, Mr. Gladstone observed that the evidence tends to show there is in progress a movement stronger than we have seen, and holds that when the change of public opinion becomes discernible it also becomes decisive. The period of inertia or balanced force is to be reckoned, not by years, but only by months. The last general election was decided in July, 1886. Before the close of the year there were six contests, making no change in the balance of parties. From January to May, 1887, there were six more con- tests. At Burnley the Liberals gained a seat; in Derby- shire the Liberal majority was increased: whilst in Ex- change Ward, Liverpool, the Liberals held their own by a majority of 27. On the other side the Tories gained no seat, whilst in West Cornwall a Radical was returned. Mr. Gladstone considers that whilst two of these elections (Burnley and Ilkeston) slowed a marked change in favour of Home Rule, the other four supplied no corre- sponding amount et countervailing evidence. Thus the second period of the present Parliament began to note the first stage of re-action. Mr. Gladstone proceeds to deal with the nine elections from the first July to the 13th August, where lie finds evidence of Us., reactirin. There were seven contested elections for seats fought in July, 1886. A portion of the seats were spontaneously laid open by Ministers who regarded them as gale. However, Spalding, Coventry, and Northwich were gained by the Liberals. Nothing could more clearly exhibit the defect of the judgment pronounced in 1886, Inch indicated not the conviction, but the perplexity of the country, for which Ire- land had paid the penalty in the Coercion Act. The year's elections yield to the Liberals a gain of four seats. Mr. Gladstone proceeds to show what effect the percentage of change would produce on the complexion of Parliament upon the assumption that it is the accidental disclosure in the particular instances of a'general change in the aggregate of the constituen- cies. This gave the promise of an excess over the com- bined Tory and Dissentient vote of 220,000. In such a figure there would be the promise of a heavy Liberal preponder- ance. A gain of 17 per cent, would give a Liberal majority of 198 in Great Britain, which, allowing the adversary credit for the whole balance of 78 uncontested seats, was reduced to 120. In conclusion Mr. Gladstone says the basis supplied by the contested elections a few months ago is too narrow to allow of demonstration or undue confidence. But viewing them in cold blood the rational Tory will probably regard them as of marked significance.

It is now ten years since this church in Butter- market-street was opened for divine worship, the Catholic Bishop of Liverpool celebrating the first Pontifidial High Mass on August 300, 1877. The church was built from the designs of the well- known Gothic architect Mr, Welby Pugin, and is 150 feet long and 55 feet wide, the roof rising to a height of over 70 feet. The spire will be 200 feet high. The interior was left to be finished at a future time owing to want of funds, but during the ten years the church has been open much has been done towards its completion. Soon after the open- ing marble rails were placed in front of the chancel, extending across the church, and a splendid marble pulpit was erected, both these works having been entrusted to Messrs Williams and Clay, of Warring- ton. When the present superior of St. Mary's came to the town, about four years ago, he at once noticed the great amount of money which must of necessity be expended before the

He contended that the Crimes Act provided that the Lord• Lieutenant should not proclaim any district unless the step was in his opinion necessary for the prevention of crime and outrage, and the Chief Secretary gave the House to understand that the Government did not intend to apply it at once to the whole of Ireland. The minutes of the Wesleyan Methodit Conference are printed, and will shortly be issued. The total membership of the Wesleyan body is given at 537,000, with nearly 47,000 on trial. The ministers number 2,887, including probationers and supernumeraries. There are 100 ministers engaged as home missionaries. DISASTER TO A PLEASURE PARTY.—Another holiday disaster is reported from Bridport. Six persons who were returning from Burton Bradstock were thrown violently to the ground by the capsizing of their vehicle, four of them being rendered insensible, -and two others injured so severely that their recovery is doubtful. One of the latter is a lady 80 years of age.

ANTICIPATED REVOLUTION DT HAVANA. Isinw Yalu, Mom:v.v.—According to advices from Key West, Havana is on the verge of revolution, owing to the action of Captain-General Mann in taking possession of. the Custom /louse, and arresting the officials on a 4iarge a/ extruPtion. The people have Strongly resisted this aqityi., and mealy condicts have taken place between the citizens and the troops, the results in some instances flaying been fatal; vhi/e nuntheri have been wounded. The city is invested with troops, and a reign of terror prevails., General Maria has issued a proclamation, commanding the troops to disperse the volunteers, and the colonels of volunteers have been ordered to disband their forces, it being evident that the mi iorlty are opposed to General Maria. Indeed, a I:, number have already joined the rioters. Cries of "Vivo Salamanca" and "Down with Mann" are frequent. A mass meeting was called for Saturday night, to protest against the conduct of the Governor-General, but the result has not yet reached here. The troops in the adjacent cities are lying on their arms, ready for the signal to advance. The Government has. seized and hold all the telegraphs.

FRESH ATTEMPT :AGAINST THE CZAR. VIENNA. FRIDAY.— A report reaches here from Berlin that on the 20th a fresh attempt was made against the Czar. It is said that a Nihilist, disguised as an officer of the Guards, succeeded in approaching the Imperial car- riage during his Majesty's journey from St. Petersburg to Krasnoe Selo. He tired two shots from a revolver. The first entirely missed, but the second perforated the Czar's coat. Ever since this event the Empress is said to have suffered ,much from nervous excitement
AYCKRICA.-WAR WITH HE RED INDIANS. -MORE EARTHQUAKE SHOCKS. . _

NEW YORK, SATORbAY.—inother war with the Red Indians is regarded as inevitable. A large party of lite Indians left the Reservation with, it is presumed, the intention of going on the war path. A large force of whites attempted to drive them back to the Reservation, but the Indians fought despe- rately from a strong position at Wolf Creek, Colorado, and successfully* resisted the attempt to drive them back to the Reservation set apart for them. Nine Indians were killed in the fight, as well as several white men. Additional troops will be sent to the dis- trict, as the greatest excitement now prevails among the Indian tribes, and it is feared that a large number will join their tribes on the warpath. Every effort is now being made to keep the Indians from leaving their Reser- vation.

'Nine YORK, SATORDAY.--Slight earthquake shocks were to-day felt in Columbia, Somerville, Charleston, South Carolina. Augusta, and Georgia districts. Although considerable alarm was occasioned, no destruction of property nor loss of life occurred. I,i2w YORK, MONDAY. Count Mitkiewitx, who left Shanghai in the early part of the month, has arrived at San Francisco, on his way to Washington, with the Chinese envoy extraordinary, bearing letters from Li flung Chung, confirming the concessions made by cer- tain Chinese companies to an American syndicate,forthe establishment of railways in China. The first railway will be between Pekin, Tien Tain, and Canton.
FRANCE.- -ANOTHER TRAGEDY.-MOBILI- SATION.

PARTS, SIINDAY.—A fearful crime was committed early this morning in the Rue Brey, a rather dingy street skirting the fashionable quarter around the Arc de Triomphe. An oculist named Francois Padrona, whose place of business is at 17, Rue Viviene, shot his wife dead wit/i a revolver, and afterwards cut the throats of his two children. The reports of the revolver aroused the neighbourhood. When the police arrived they found the murderer in the cellar. His behaviour when arrested suggested the idea of real or feigned insanity. Padrona is a German, 35 years of age. His wife was several years younger. Happily the murderer forgot the little baby, scarcely three months old, who was found sleeping tranquilly by the side of the dead mother. PAS/S. Mosruiv.—Two soldiers, who have been acting as secretaries to the Minister of War, were arrested this morning. The charge against them is one of high trea- son, they having, it is alleged, communicated to the Figaro the plan of mobilisation of the Seventeenth Army Corps. THE NEW CANADIAN FISHERIES COM.

div.head: MISSION.
div.p: MISSION.

OTTAWA, WDDNESDAY.-With regard to the appointment of a Joint Commission by Great Britain and the United States for the settlement of the fisheries dispute,it is under- stood that in addition to Mr. Chamberlain, Her Majesty's Government will appoint Sir L. Becky'lle West, British Minister at Washington, to act on the Commission, and that Canada will be invited to appoint the third Cotemiesioner, who will in all probability be Sir J. Macdonald. The Cana- dian Premier served on the Alabama Commiasion, which met at Washington in 1871. It is expected that the new Commission will sit in the capital of the United States. A RUSSIAN MISSION ATTACKED.

___,.... BOMBAY, THURSDAY. - Intelligence has been received here from Badakshan that a Ruseian mission to Kashgar has been compelled to return to Khokand in Ferghans owing to some of the members of the mission having insulted Moslem women. It is added that a few Russians were killed. , RESIGNATION OF THE BULGARIAN

div.head: MINISTRY.
div.p: MINISTRY.

A Central News telegram, from Vienna on Thursday, says that immediately before the signing of the decree sanc- tioning the new Ministry, by Prince Ferdinand, at Sofia, on Wednesday, the Cabinet met and resolved to tender their resignation, owing to the dissatisfaction prevailing amongst the Powers regarding the present position of Bul- garian affairs.

div.head: CURRENT POLITIC
div.p: CURRENT POLITIC

On Monday, Mr. Osborne Morgan, M.P., and Mr. W. Abraham, M.P., addressed a mass meeting of miners at Rhos-Llanerchrugog. near Wrexham. Mr. Morgan said the Mines Regulation BhIJ. if Passed by the House of Lords as amended, would relieve the barrenness of the present session. He looked upon it as a good measure, calculated to improve the condition of miners.—Mr. Abraham said no amount of legislation would do much good for the miners unless they were united. Let them organise and be determined to act together, and they would aChieve the objects they desired. Union among themselves was essential to their improvement. A demonstration, convened by the Liberal League to denounce the action of the Government in proclaiming the National League, was held in Trafalgar7square, London, on Saturday evening. Contingents from the Liberal and Radical Associatiodrs, branches of the National League, and trade and other societies in London, marched With bands and banners to the square, where there were four platforms. The speakers included Messrs. Biggar, pip, Shirley, MY, Quinn, M.P., and Joseph Nolan, MY., and a Protestant clergyman frpm Ulster also denounced the policy of the Government, and said the people ot Ulster were coming round to the principle of home Rule. 'The following resolution was unanimously adopted :—" That this meeting of working men of the metropolis condemns in the strongest possible manner the proclamation of the Irish National League as an iniquitous interference with the right to combination, and considera it the duty of all to support the National. League in resisting the operation of the Coercion Act." The proceeding‘were orderly throughout, and attracted little general attention.
THE . PROCLAMATION DIVISION.-AEALYSIS OF

THE VOTING. In the division on Mr. Gladstone's motion, in opposi- tion to the. proclamation of the National League, the following votes were given:— Bight Liberal Unionists voted in the minority of 194 against the Government—Messrs. T. R. Buchanan, J. Chamberlain, R. Chamberlain, Jew Collings, B. Hingley, W. Kenrick, J. P. Williams. and A. J. Winterbotham. Sir Hussey Vivian also voted for Mr. Gladstone's motion.

The Liberal Unionists voting in the majority with the Government were :—Mr. 11. T. Anstruther, Viscount Baring, Messrs. Alfred Barnes, rHamet, Bass, H. F. Beaumont, Bickford Smith, Iliddul`ph, B6litho, J. Bright, R. Campbell, Lord E. Cavendish, Mr. Coghill, Mr. J. Cor- bett, Gen. Crossman, Sir D. Currie, Viscount Ebrington ; Messrs. Arthur Elliot, Flueli F. Elliot, Finlay, Fitz- wiLliam, L. Fry; Sir T. Grove, the Marquis of Harling- ton, Mr. Hastings, Sir Havelock Allan, Mr. Robhouse, Mr. Thomas Lea, Sir John Lubbock; Messrs. T. W. Maclean, Storey, Maskelvne, F. Mildmay, W. Morrison, T. Richardson, Baron F. De Rothschild, Messrs. T. W. Russell, Craig Sellar, T. Sutherland. F. Taylor, Greville, Vernon, Sir E. Watlan, Messrs. Cornwallis West, Wiggin, Wodehouse, and Viscount Wolmer. Forty-seven Union- ists, Including Mr. John Corbett and Sir E. Watkin, thus supported the Government No Liberals voted in the Majority, and no Conserva- tives in the minority. An analysis of the division shows that 101 Gladstonians, 85 Nationalists, and nine Liberal Unionists supported Mr. Gladstone. The majority con- sisted of 227 Conservatives and 45 Liberal Unionists.

Mr. James Dixon was on Thursday installed Master of the Sheffield Cutlers' Company, and in the evening he gave the usnaP banquet in the Cutlers' Hall. Owing to the breakdown of a Great-Western engine at St. James' Park Station, district railway, on Tbur3- day morning, traffic was delayed about 25 minutes. Mr. Chamberlain will proceed, as has been arranged, to Ireland in October, and will address one or more meetings In the north. In November next he will leave England for America to discharge his duties on the Fishery Com- mission. Addressing a meeting of his constitients at Dungannon, on Thursday, Mr. T. W. Russell, M.P , said he had left the Parliamentary organisation of the Liberal Unionists as a protest against the "maiming and wounding " of the Land Bill in the House of Lords. He had not seceded from the party., and did not intend to join Mr. Gladstone. SEIZURE OF A BRITISH SEALING BCHOONER.—Another British sealing schooner has been seized as a prize by a United States Revenue cutter, for alleged illegal fishing in Bebring's Straits. Her.papers and firearms and cargo of seal skins were taken on board the cutter, and the schooner ordered to proceed to Sitka. Her captain, however, ran for Victoria, British Columbia. Instead, arriving there on Weds nesday morning.

div.head: GENERAL NEWS.
div.p: GENERAL NEWS.
On Sunday, Tom Hackett, once a noted prizefighter, fell down and expired suddenly in Crown-court, Fleet- street, London. Heart disease is the supposed cause of death. _ _ _

Orders were received at Portsmouth Dockyard, on Mon- day, directing the discharge in 14 days' time of another 300 men. It is understood that about 200 of these will be shipwrights. Mr. Gladstone on Saturday journeyed from London to Hawarden. The ea-Premier travelled in a saloon car- riage, and was accompanied by Mr. Herbert Gladstone, M.P., and Mr. Henry Gladstone. _ _

On Monday, 31 fever cases were admitted into the hos- pitals of the Metropolitan Board. There are now under treatment 881 cases, of which 802 were scarlet fever, one typhus, 74 enteric, and four other diseases. The death- rate is small.

The strike amongst the labourers at the Terminus (Glasgow) Harbour has been settled, the stevedores allowing the men to resume work at the old rate oi wages. The employers had sought to reduce wages one penny per hour. According to the report just issued the total number of members of the Primitive Methodist Church is now 191,662, with 2,038 ministers. The denomination pos- sesses 4,392 chapels, with sittings for 931,149 people, erected at an outlay of £2,649,477 2s. 6d.

The various barristers appointed to hold Revision Courts over England and Wales for the purpose of revis- ing the Parliamentary voters' lists will hold their respec- tive courts to bear borough claims between September 15 and October 31, while county claims will be heard between September 20 and October 31. DEATH OF SIR FRANCIS Haan. The death of Si? Francis Head, Bart., was announced on Monday. The deceased was born in 1817, and succeeded his father as second baronet in 1875. He was in the service of the Honourable East India Company from 1835 to 1843. He is succeeded by his son Robert Garnett, who was born in 1845.

WEASELS FOR AUSTRALIA.—During the past week a consignment of stoats and weasels, numbering upwards of 250, collected by Mr. Allbones, of Brigg, have been despatched to London, en route for Australia. This is the ninth shipment of these animals Mr. Alltymes has forwarded to that colony, and he has orders for 1,000 more. They are being exported for the purpose of de- stroying rabbits, which overrun the colony and make much havoc amongst the crops.

Disgusted with the charges and innuendoes brought against the Leek Fire Brigade in connection with the re- cent fire at Mr. Booth's tannery, Captain Carding and the whole of the brigade have resigned. The complaints of Mr. Booth, who was uninsured', have been investigated by the Leek Improvement Commissioners, who com- pletely exonerated the brigade. Mr. Booth, however, has reiterated the charges, with the result stated. The brigade was one of the smartest in the country, and has won in- ternational prizes. A WOMAN DECAPITATED ON THE RAILWAY.—On Satur- day evening the headless body of a woman was dis- covered lying upon the London and North-Western Company's -- in line between the Leeds and New Wort- ley stations, ..bout a mile from the former place. A search was made for the woman's head, which was ulti- mately found some distance from where the body was lying. The remains turned out to be those of Ann Foss- wick, a single woman, aged 56 years, of New Wortley. It has not transpired how she got upon the line. SHOCKING TRAMWAY FATALITT.--011 Monday, mother and daughter were walking along the Southend Pier, when they heard a tramcar coming behind them, and, becoming confused, got oil, the wrong side of the line, with the result that the mßtlier. was crushed to death between the pier and the side of the car, while the daughter received such injury that she was conveyed bp special train to London, for removal to hospital. The parties were excursionists from London. The daughter's injuries are considered dangerous.

NEW DEPARTHRII IN THR IRISH BAPTIST CHURCH.—Dr. Clifford and the Rev. Charles Williams, who have been visiting the Irish Baptist Churches on behalf of the Baptist Union, met a number of the pastors in Belfast to confer on the future prospects and working in Ireland. Some gra,stic elwg_es in the line of denominational Home Rule are foreshadowed, but of course nothing= be settled until the autumnal meetings of the Union, to be held in Sheffield in October next. We hear that great anxiety, not to say alarm, has been caused in some War- tars by this suggested new departure, and much wisdom will be needed to reconcile conflicting interests and pilot the scheme safely through.—British Weekly.

EXTRAORDINARY SUICIDE OF A Soitcrroa.--Con- siderable sensation was caused in Birmingham, on Saturday, by the intelligence that Mr. J. Fisher, a member of the well-known firm of Messrs. Unett, Page, and Fisher, solicitors, had shop himself, in his own office. fie was found lying on his office floor, with a bullet wound in his right temple, and a revolver lying near his hand. Medical assistance was procured, and he was conscious at intervals; and in reply to an inquiry said be did not know how it was done. He soon Suc- cumbed. Deceased was solicitor to Sir Alfred Gooch, and married a daughter of Mr. Alfred Hickman, ironmaster. Wolverhampton. The cause of his suicide is not at pre- sent known. -

POISONED AT A WEDDING FEAST.—Portions Of It leg of mutton used at the wedding feast at Winsford,Cheshire, which caused the death of one person, Mrs. Blagg, son., and produced serious vomiting and purging on all the other guests, some 14 or 15 in number, have been sub- mitted to Mr. Blades, analytical chemist, of Northwich, for examination. Mr. Blades could discover no traces of mineral poison in the leg of mutton. but a change in the structure of the fibres led him to search for evidence of a class of poisons called ptomaine, with the result that lie found the hypothesis to be well founded. The poison, Mr. Blame explains, is one which is de- veloped by the action of certain micro-organisms that have only recently been studied by scientists.

SEVEN CIINTKNARTANS IN Ors DlSTRlCT.—Particulars are furnished of no less than seven remarkable cases of longevity in the province of Astrachan. They are all the more extraordinary from the fact that Astrachan is con- sidered to be a very unhealthy district. The following persons of the peasant class died in that province last year, all being more than 100 years of age :—John 'Moos- loff, 105 years, of the village of Prishib : Dania Abolyaninoff, 105 years, of the Cossack settlement of Krasnoyarsk; Simon Kharkoff, 110, of the village of Ikrian ; Jessy Lissenko and Cyril Theftehenko, of the villages of Feodorofka and Vladimirofka respectively, both 110 years; John I3ootkolf, of the village of Jorgovia, 114 years; and Andrew Novtchopersky, of the village of Kisolovo, 120 years old.

SWIMMING MATCH IN SWEDEN.—VICTORY OF AN ENG- LISH LADY.—On Sunday afternoon, the 14th inst., in the lake at Nackanas, Stockholm, a swimming match took place for the one mile championship of Sweden. The first prize was a very fine gold medal. There were seven competitors—five gentlemen and two ladies, one of whom was Miss Theresa Johnson, the "Lady Champion Swimmer of England," and bravely she upheld her re- putation. At half a mile two of the gentlemen gave up, and at three-quarters ot a mile two more, leaving only Miss Johnson, Mr. Hanson, and Miss Andersen, who iS only thirteen or fourteen years of age. Miss Johnson eventually won by 220 yards from Mr. Hanson, and about 500 from Miss Andersen, in 30min. 2sec. Miss Johnson swam the whole course with a splendid over- hand stroke, and everyone at Stockholm says there has never been such fine swimming before. PsizsoNat AND POINTRD.—It is said that Mr. Spurgeon is in the habit of testing the abilities of the more promis- ingnf his students of his college by obliging them to go up into the pulpit with a sealed envelope in their hands, containing the text of their address. On one of these occasions a student, on opening the paper, found this sub- ject set, "Apply the story of Zacahreus to your own per- sonal qualifications and call." And he delivered himself in the following way :—" My brethren, the subject on which I have to address you to-day is a comparison between Zacchieus and my cwn qualifications. Well, the first thing we read about Zacclueus was. that he was small of stature, and I never felt so small as I do now. In the second place we read that he climbed up into a tree, which is very much my position now. Thirdly, we read that Zacchtens 'made haste to come down,' in which I joyfully follow his example."

KISSING BY • SEXTON.—At Dartford Petty Sessions, on Saturday, Joseph Dean, sexton in the employ of the Dartford Burial Board, was charged with assaulting a girl named Emily Holland. The prosecutrix, a domestic servant in the employ of Mrs. Winch, was sent to attend to some flowers on a grave in the Dartford temetery, and while she was engaged in watering the plants de- fendant came up, kissed her, and otherwise assaulted her. When proseentrix's mother went to see defendant about the matter, Mrs. Dean said to her husband, "This is a frequent occurrence ; 'why don't you leave the girls alone?" Defendant's wife also said that hor husband was in the habit of kissing young girls who came into the cemetery because they liked it; and Mrs. Holland said in future he had better not take French leave as some girls did not like kissing.—Thadefendant was fined 408, and costs.—Defendant, who had denied the charge altogether, asked theta term ot imprisonment might be imposed, in order that he might appeal avbainst the con- viction; but the magistrates would not entertain the request.

REFUSAL TO DELIVIIR RAILWAY TICKETS.-At the Guildhall Police Court, on Monday, Henry Young, who gave an address at 64, Vicarage-road, Tottenham, was charged on remand, before Alderman Gray, with having refted to deliver up a railway ticket when requested to do so, and also with assaulting a ticket-inspector in the (service of the Metropolitan Railway Company. Mr. Walter Beard appeared for the defendant, and quoted several cases in which the judges had held that a railway company's servants had no right to demand tickets from passengers after they had left the train. Tickets must be demanded either in the train or before the passengers entered it. Mr. Hopkinson, who appeared for the com- pany, contended that the collector had a perfect right to detain the prisoner on the non-production of the ticket, for without it bow could he tell whether. or not the de- fendant had paid his fare, or whether the company WU being defrauded? Alderman Gray said he regretted that be was unable to decide in this case. He hoped there would soon be an alteration in the law on that point. :Mr. Hopkinson applied for leave to appeal, which Mr. Alderman Gray readily gave.

The third butter and crire-se factory Ili :•,cuLhatui 13 about to be started at Dolphington by a limited liability company, with a capital of £2,500. It is stated that in all likelihood the transfer of the Im- perial remains from Chislehurst to Farnborough Hill will be unattended by any special ceremony.

A man was discovered lying on the rails at Bolton- street Railway Station, Bury, on Saturday morning, with a portion of his head cut away by the wheels of a pas- sing train. Deceased appeared to be about 40 years of age- Dxsynnerret FIRE /It SALFORD.—ShortIy before three a.m. on Monday, a ire was discovered to have broken out at the extensive premises of the Messrs. Haworth, dyers and finishers, Ordeal-lane, Salford. The damage is roughly estimated at £2,000. At • special petty sessions at Harlesden 1,400 sum- ‘monses were made returnable at the instance of the Willesden board for arrears of rates amounting in the ag- gregate to about £4,000. The bench made a general order for payment in 14 days. dff the Royal Naval College, Greenwich, at low tide, the edge of the Thames for several yards is as black as ink, and at other times the water is very dirty and offen- sive. At Woolwich the river has the appearance of liquid sewage. There is a sickening smell from the water. The injury to property in the Cheshire salt district has of late become so enormous that a movement for obtaining compensation from the brine pumpers has been resuscitated. A deputation of property owners hada= interview with Mr. Brunner, M.P., on Saturday, when he promised that he would endeavour to get a Royal Commission appointed to inquire into the matter. The books in the library of one of our greater insti- tutions having been affected by damp, a practical chemist has been consulted; and he says:—" Quicklime is the best thing imaginable to save books from the ill- effects of damp. A small vessel full of lime placed near a bookcase is better than a blazing fire for this purpose. The lime must be changed every two or three days." A very considerable demand for iron and steel has been experienced in South Staffordshire within the last few days. Foreign buyers are offering heavy orders for bars and sheets, and local consumers are anxious co buy large hive of common sheets of 2,000 and 3,000 tons, but manufacturers ask more money. Orders for steel are re- fused through the inability of manufacturers to deliver within the required time.

Sir Edward Watkin intends, during the recess, to take steps for the purpose of ascertaining the practicability of constructin<, a submarine tunnel between the Mull of Cantyre in Scotland and Fair Bead in Ireland. The two points are only about 10 miles apart. One drawback to the advantages of such a tunnel scheme is the fact that the Mull of Cantyre is less accessible from any populous part of Scotland than any part of the north of Ireland.

A t3corrisu NATIONAL LEAGUE.—A deputation of Irish members Of Parliament, including either Mr. John Dillon or Mr. Sexton, will attend the conference at Oban on the 15th September, when the desirability of forming Scottish National League for promoting Rome Rule, land law, and other reforms for Scotland will be dis- cussed. It is understood that the movement has tho approval of the majority of the Scottish Gladstonian members.

An amusing srene was witnessed at Deal the other morning. The herd of elephants, comps/sing eight huge beasts, connected with Sanger's menagerie, were taken down to the sea for a bath. As soon as the animals reached the water they began to disport themselves in a most curious fashion, spouting the water at each other and evident/y greatly enjoying their bath, much to the amusement of the throngs of visitors who watched them from the shore.

TEE TRAGEDY AT FONTYPRIDD.—At the Pontypridd Police Court, on Saturday, the prisoner, Thoina.s Morgan, charged 'with the murder of Morgan Salathiel and with wounding 13 othet persons, was remanded until to- day pending the close of the coroner's inquiry. Three of the injured persons, two of whom were shot in the bowels, are still in a precarious condition. It is Stated that the prisoner Morgan in his fury fired nearly 300 pellets into the crowd. SERI.OI7S FIRES IN MYTTINGRAM.—Two serious fires oc- curred in Nottingham on Sunday afternoon,one at Messrs. Drapers' printing establishment, resulting in damage amounting to upwards of £2,000. Two firemen, while working on the ground floor of the building, were buried in the burning debris, the two upper floors giving way suddenly and the building collapsing. Both were badly burped and otherwise injured, but fatal results are not inticipated. At the same time' another fire was dis- covered in premises a short distance away, wherefrom 20 horses were with difficulty rescued. Eighteen vans were destroyed. Three other fires were reported in Not- tingham and the district last night, but the damage was Small _ - PAINFUL TRAGEDY IN YORESIIIRE.—A sad affair occurred in Winding-road. Halifax, on Saturday night. A married woman named Susannah Marriott, 39 years of age, had been recently confined, and had a child five weeks old. She was being attended to by her mother, Mrs. Sarah Mills, who resides in Leeds. About seven o'clock Mrs. Mills left her daughter and grandchild in the house for a little while. On her return her daughter was in the act of attempting to hang herself. Mrs. Mills was fortu- nate enough to prevent her, and managed to get her back to bed. On looking round for the baby, she was shocked to find it drowned in the washing tub, where it had been Immersed by its mother. Mrs. Marriott's mind is said to be affected as the result of the confinement. A RAILWAY STATION DESTROYED BY FISOL—A fire broke out on Saturday evening in the lamproom of the Tavi- stock Station on the Plymouth and Launceston branch of the Great Western Railway, and raged so furiously that from the first there was little chance of saving any portion of the passenger station. The building was com- pletely gntred. Before the flames were subdued, the booking-office and the station-master's and inspector's offices we.re burnt to the ground, and the refreshment. room and parcel-office were unnofed. The station pro- per, a large wood and glass structure, was almost entirely destroyed. Two men named James Waldron, a ritter, and John Warner, a smith, were seriously in- SAD BOATING CALAMITY: Loss OF FIVE DIVES.—OR Sunday afternoon a shocking disaster occurred on the Humber, wherby five lives were lost Four men, named William Fish, Alfred Elson, William Thorpe, and Richard Scarr, all of Hull, and a man whose name is un- known, left Hull in a boat and crossed the river to Bar- ton-on-Humber, Lincolnshire, where they remained until half-past three, when they were joined by two other men, the names of whom are not known. They kept together to return to Hull, and were off New Holland, when, accord- ing to tha statement of Fish, they attempted to change oars, and the movement caused the boat to capsize, throwing all the seven into the water. They clung to the boat for some time, but five of them became exhausted, and one by one relinquished their hold and were carried away by the tide and drowned. Only two were saved, those being Fish and Elson, who were not seen until an hour and a half had elapsed. They were then picked up In an exhausted condition, and taken to Hull.

THE YACHTING DISASTER AT ILFRACOMBE. -- Up to Saturday afternoon only five bodies had been recovered at Ilfracombe. The inquest on the bodies re- covered was opened on Saturday. They were identified as Mr. Samuel Walker, aged 53, The Elms, Edmonton; Mr.- Pinker, one of the firm of Duck,' Son, and Pinker, Bath; Mr. W. Wareham, aged 65, merchant, Charing Cross, London; Mr. George Turner, Lansdown-road, Beth; and Miss Annie Ash, court dressmaker, 111, Bond- street, London.—Wm. Rumson, boatman, stated that the pleasure yacht Monarch was about ten tons register, and left on Friday afternoon with a party of twenty- two persons, exclusive of the crew. The sea was not rough, but the weather was squally. Everything went right Until they got about half-a-mile from land, when a gust of wind struck the yacht and put her gunwale under water. The boat-hook then slipped .overboard, and the yacht was put about to piek it up. A sudden gust of wind blew the boom over, and the yacht heeled over, filled, and sank. The Coroner, in summing up, said that the disaster seemed to be a pure accident,! Mr. Francis Windsor, of Southport, and Mr. Thos. smith, of 48. Buckingham Palace-road, London, are among the missing. A subscription list is being raised for the widow and family of Buckingham, the boatman.—There is now, no doubt that others besides those known were on board the Ilfracombe yacht. Twenty-six were on board, and 17 were rescued, five of whom have died. An attempt has been made to raise the yacht, but no traces of other bodies have been found.

SINGULAR Rita LEE CELETIRAT I ON.—On Saturday the Queen's Jubilee was celebrated in a novel fashion at Denby Dale, near Barnsley. Denby Dale has for a long time been celebrated for its pies. In 1788 there was one baked in commemoration of King George the Third's recovery ; another was baked in 1815 in honour of the peace; and the third was in 1848 in celebration of the repeal of the Corn Laws; and now a pie has been baked which is described as 'without equal in the annals of pie making. On Saturday a crowd of people flocked to Denby Dale from Bradford, Huddersfield, Barnsley. Penistone, -and the small villages 'within a radius of eight or nine miles, and ea rfy before noon people took up a position outside the farriers which had been erected to keep off the crush whi'o the old people of the village Of Denby Dale and the school children of Denby, Denby Dale, and Cumberworth were being served with portions sof-the pie. The baking took plaee in a special oven, and tbepterwaseft. in disinetorand 21t. deep, and contained 64 stones of sour, I,BSollis. of beef, 180 lbs, of mutton, 1601bs. of real, isms. of lamb, 250115. of pork, 1201bs, of lard, 801 b. of butter, 32 couples of rabbits, 3 hares, 42 fowls. 40-plgeons, 12 grouse, 21 ducks, 4 plovers, 1 turkey, 5 geese,.and 100 small birds; together with 30 eggs and4o atones of potatoes, 401 b. of beef suet, and 401 b. of drip. The The pie weighed about two tons five or six cwt. t morning it was ttzlzen on a stone cart, drawn by ten horses, to a field calhtti Norman Park. Directly the roe ha 4 been taken under one end of the tent in 'which it vast) be served to the people. the strong wooden bar- Miles against which the crowd pressed gave way, and inning multitudes rushed into the tent up to the stone curt, sod there ensued a scene of great confusion. In 'vain were the people appealed to. The stronger the lloommai the Ore th craished into the tent, and the '..:74-;t7Topidly disappeared, being either given or forcibly ita-kou away, and it was not until a promise had been ioaae'tbat when the old people and children had been served the pie should be brought into the field and dis- , trilauted, that the hungry mob Would be appeased. In the evening there was a dibplay of fireworks.
EXECUTION OF A WIFE MURDERER.- A LIGHT-HEARTED CULPRIT.

William Wilton, wheelwright, for the murder of his wife, at Brighton, ,on July 9th, was executed in Lewes Gaol, on Monday. Wilton passed a good night, rose at half-past six, made a hearty breakfast, and was attended by the chaplain. Me appeardd to be %ate indifferent to his fate, and left no expression of sorrow. Berry, the hangman, spent Sunday in Brightens and slept in the Eatki. The prison bell commenced tolling at a quarter to nine o'clocl, On the executioner proceeding to pinion Wilton, the latter shook hands with him, and bade him "Good morning," and "Good-bye;" and then bade all the warders" Good-bye." Just before nine o'clock the pro- cession emerged from the prison into the yard, the chaplain leading, and reading the service. Wilton walked firmly to execution,betweeu two warders. Berry directed the condemned man on to the trap door, and quickly adjusted the cap, strapped his legs, and pulled the bolt. Wilton disappeared from view, and died almost instan- taneously. There was a slight swaying of the rope, and a little muscular tremor. Wilton weighed 9st. 4 lbs. and a sft. drop was allowed. The clock struck nine just after he disappeared from view. There were about 150 people outside the gaol when the black flag was hoisted. The condemned man's conduct was very good whilst in prison. The usual inquest followed.

div.head: IRELAND.
div.p: IRELAND.

On MondaY, a Privy Conncil was held in Dublin Castle, in relation to ihe proclamation of the National League. The Lord-Lieuton•lnt presided, and amongst those present was Lord Ashbourne, who arrived in Dublin in the morning, having beenburriedly summoned from Boulogne to attend the meeting. A telegram on Monday reported a shooting outrage at Bilmurry, West Clare. Shots were fired into the houses of several farmers who are suspected of having paid their rents, although they subscribed to the Plan of Campaign. A farmer named Griffin had a narrow escape. the shot lodging in the posts of the bed where he slept. Mr. Gardiner, R.M, attended at the Cork County Gaol on Monday, and a further remand was granted for a week of the case in which Dr. Cross is charged with poisoning his wife at Shandy Hall, Coachfonl, on the 2nd June last. It is believed that the Crown case will be completed on Monday next, and it is stated that some startling evidence will then be adduced.

The Lord Lieutenant has proclaimed as "an illegal as- sembly "the great Nationalist meeting summoned for Sun- day en Ballvcoree Hill, county Clare. TRH PROCLAIMED LFAGUIL—ADMISSIOM OF ENGLISH MEMBERS —The first meeting of the central branch of the National League since Its proclamation was held, on Time- day, in Dublin. The attendance was unusually large. A large number of English gentlemen were proposed for mem- bership, including Messrs. Convbeare and Schwann, M.Prt. A telegram was read from Mr. Davitt, asking to be excused for non-attendanc•. Mr. William O'Brien, who presided, said that very likely the League would suppress the Tory Ministry. The Government must not be allowed to sup. press the right of free speech ; the Government must not be allowed to interfere with the tenant's combination; and they must not be allowed to victimise the tenants who bad adopted the Plan of Campaign. The people had a perfect right to combine against rack-renters and land grabbers.
PROPOSED CONFERENCE OF IRISH LANDLORDS AND TENANTS.

Archbishop Walsh, in a letter to the Freeman's Journal. says The formation of a representative council, as the result of the meeting of landlords and incumbrances, suggests the possibility that effective steps may be take* towards the settlement of the hind 'lineation. For such settlement, they must look to those who on one side or other are personally interested, rather than to the offi- cial deliberations of any English statesmen. Why should they not bring together a Round Table' Con- ference of accredited or recognised representatives of the landlords and tenants, to trace, at all events, the out- lines of a solution? Arrangements could be made within a month."

_ Mr. Wentworth Erck, hon. secretary of the Landlords' and Incumbrancers' AssociAtion, has written to the Freeman's Joltrital, as an Trish landlord, most heartily concurring with Archbishop liakh in the suggestion that "the basis of a compromise between the landlorda and tenants should he settled by us Trish here in Ireland. rather than by English and Scotch politicians. We are now but, as it *ere, mortgagees of estates once-our own, and for the deterioration occasioned by the legislature we maintain that we have a title to compensation; and we cannot listen to proposals fOr a further confiscation Of our property." - BAILIFFS AND POLICE REPTILSP.D.

The evictions on the O'Grady estate, at Rerbertstown, commenced on Tuesday, a force of 130 police and 50 men of the Leinster Regiment being present, in charge of Capt. Plunkett, divisional resident magistrate. John Carroll was evicted without opposition, but considerable resistance was offered when it was attempted to evict a widow named Cremms, at. Kilballyowen. :Arnim were thrown directly the bailiffs approached, and when the officers of the law attempted to effect an entrance by a gable window they were repulsed with boiling water. Three bailiffs then mounted the roof, and worked with hatchets and crowbars, until ,a hole waa made, but then they were attacked by the inmates with iron bars, and were compelled to retreat- A hole was then made in the back of the house, but boiling water again forced the bailiffs back. The police then rushed forward to the aperture, but again a volume of scalding water was thrown, and they fell back. In- another moment, however, they had fixed bayonets, and the bailiffs then entered with a rush, the police following directly afterwards. The inmates, consisting of live men and four women, were arrested, and conveyed to gaol, singing " God.save Ireland ! " The greatest, excitement prevailed outside during the eviction, and the police die- persed the people with their batons several times.

div.head: DEFIANT SPEECHES AT CORK.
div.p: DEFIANT SPEECHES AT CORK.

The first meeting of the Cork National League since the issuing of the Government proclamation was held on Monday. Some policemen and detectives were stoned outside the Assembly Rooms, where the meeting was held, and persons entering the building were scrutinised.. The Mayor presided, and the attendance was very large.. It was first arranged to hold the meeting in a small hall, but the crush was so grelt that it was decided to adjourn to:a larger hall. Immediately a rush was made for the. large hall, and-the crush was here also so great that the crowd invaded the platform, and much delay was caused before order could be restored. Anion7st those present were Mr. M. Healy, M.P., Mr. Ogles, M.P., together with three or four Englishmen. . . -

The MAYOR, in-opening the proceedings, remarked on the extraordinarily largo attendance, although the meet- ing was only an ordinary one. In view of the recent proclamation, the demonstration of enthusiasm was sig- nificant in the highest degree. It showed that no amount of proclamations could intimidate the people. The time bad arrived when the people would have to face the. prison cell. He would say that they approached the struggle with a light heart and with the consciousness that on their action would depend the salvation of the Irish people. If the Cork National League had been proclaimed, it would not, he believed, have lessened in the least the attendance. There was only room for fifty in the Cork prison, and the people there that night would fill all the gaols in Ireland. If the struggle be- came fiercer, why, the people would warm to the fight. From his experience of the country, he felt sure that all economic rent had disappeared this year. Mr. M. Eleamr M.P., said that when the Coercion Act was passing through Parliament the Irish members told. the Government that they would wipe their boots with their proclamations, and that great meeting was a proof of the truth of what the Irish members.had said. Thet Irish people had the English democracy at its back, and the Irish people flouted and despised the Government.. The National League had been proclaimed as dangerous., It was dangerous as regards the landlords, and it would' continuo to be a danger to "le landlords. The justifica— tion of the National League was written on the Statute-book of tlie realm. It looked as if the Irish people were about to have a hot winter.. The men who faced the gallows and the trans-. portation hulks would not fly away from the present. miserable Government. Let their enemies come on.; They were anxious that the struggle should come imme- diately if it was to come at all. They owed to the Coer— cion Act the enlightening of the English neople that, there was no midway between con( illation and coercion. , The Coercion Act would lead to much hardship and ini-1 prisonment, but he believed that in the end it would' prove a blessing in disguise. Ho proposed the following resolution :.--"That we regard the proclamation of the. National League as an act of high-handed tyranny, and; that we declare our determination to resist the unconsti-.1 tutional proceedings of the Government by every meansl in our power." The resolution was carried with great enthusiasm.

It is stated that on the door of a room in one ot the colleges of Oxford there is to'be found a very interesting combination of well-known political names. They are "Mr. Peel," "Mr. Gladstone," arid" Mr. Disraeli." The three students are respectively the son of the Speaker and grandson of the great Sir Robert Peel, the grand- nephew of Mr. Gladstone, aria the nephew and heir of the late Lord Beaconsfield.

without asking that the magistrates shall, by granting a new license, put some hundreds of pounds in their pockets. As to the condi- tional offer to give up licenses in certain quarters, it is pretty well known that this is because these houses do not pay their way as , they are expected to do; and the proper thing is, under these circumstances, to let them die a natural death. If there are fewer licensed houses there will be less drinking, And there is plenty of room, as yet, for im- provement—judging from the kind of cases which were tried by the magistrates on Mon- day. The men in Warrington seem to have taken a turn for the better; but it is appalling to reflect that there has been an enormous in- crease in female drunkenness during the past ten yeats. According to the Chief Constable's returns, 592 males were in 1878 convicted of drunkenness; in 1887 the number was 332, show- ing a satisfactory reduction of from +o to 5o per cent. But with regard to the women of the town, the very reverse of this has happened. In 1878 the number of females convicted of drunkenness was 81; in 1887 it was 168. _ .

The increase, it will be observed, is over roo per cent in ten years! Need we say that in view of a fact so startling every effort should be made by citizens who have the well being of the community at heart to seek to diminish rather than increase the facilities for obtain-

.._.....,. ....... ing intoxicating liquor. Mr. DAVIES thinks the large amount of drunkenness amongst the females of Warrington is due to their get- ting "better wages than were received in most places." But we cannot accept this. ex- planation, for in the cotton manufacturing districts of East Lancashire, where females re-
ceive high wages, there is much less female drunkenness than in this part of Lancashire.
Again, how does Mr. DAVIES explain the increase_ of _drunkenness in .Warrington ?

_ Surely he will not argue that the women are receiving higher wages than they obtained in 1878, when convictions amongst females were less by one half? There has been great corn- plaint during the past ten years of depression of trade, and the women workers of the dis- trict have felt the pinch as well as the men. The more likely cause of the increase of female drunkenness is to be found in the sys- tem of off licenses. We are reaping where we ha':e sown ; we have made it easier for women to get drink, and we have more drunken women. Another point worthy of

I consideration is that there is little or no pro- vision in Warrington for the intellec- tual recreation of the gentle sex. In other towns young women have access to a Free Library: but in Warrinzton the Library is not free, and such provision as is made for reading at the Library is of zaurse in the in- terest of the lords of creation. IC seems to be thought, "with the baibarous Turk," that "woman has nevcr a soul to save;" but some day or other, when the deterioration of the' mothers has made its -lf felt on the children. we shall awake from the present stupor and endeavour to repair the wrong which has been done. But it may then be too late; now is the accepted time; now is the day nt sal- vation.

Mr. GLADSTONE has contrived to make an interesting speech on Her Majesty's .rubilee when everything in reference to the Jubilee has become tabooed as tiresome. On Tues- day., he gave a dinner to the aged people in the parish of Hawarden, and after dinner he delivered an address which many of the old folks would enjoy more than the dinner it- self. Mr. GLADSTONE, as he reminded his hearers, is amongst the number of those who came into the world before the Jubilee of GEORGE III; and it is of interest to have it on his authority that so far as the masses of the people are concerned, there is no com- parison between the celebration of the Ju- bilee of 1887 and that of 181 r. One was thoroughly popular, while the other was thoroughly official. Apart from regard or disregard to the reigning sovereign, the fact that the people, as a whole, are much better off than they were at the beginning of the present century has much to do with the character as well as the extent of their re- joicings. In the old days—so often fool- ishly spoken of as "the good old times " , when, as Sir JoHN GLyNN has it, "the poor starved and were hanged," there was little ground. for jubilation that any particular sovereign had reigned for 5o years. Capital punishment was administered with a freedom which seemed to suggest that there was no idea of any .better way of reforming k criminal than by putting him out of exist- eece. Boys and girls were hanged, as well as men and women, for offences which, as Mr. GLADSTONE says, we should hardly think now- a-days of punishing with smart corporal chastisement. Truly the road to knowledge in these matters has been trodden in bitter- ness and in pain. The lesson of humane dealing and of trust in the people has been slowly learned; and even now so far as Ire- land is concerned there are politicians who think that an ever-and-ever Coercion Act is better for that country than everlasting Home: Rule. After commenting on the great im- provement in the material condition of the people Mr. GLADSTONE said "the, great mass of those happy and blessed changes isj associated with the name and the action of t the Queen."
