ON Tuesday it was announced in the House of Commons that a Commission was being constituted by the Governments of England and the United States to deal with the dis- puted question of the North American Fisheries ; but the most interesting feature of the information was the statement that Mr. CHAMBERLAIN is to be chief Commissioner on behalf of this country. He is undoubtedly well qualified for the task ; he has great aptitude for grasping new facts and dealing with masses of detail ; and he is exceed- ingly tenacious of his opinion when once it is formed. He is, indeed, too unyielding where personal pride has play; but, acting as a Commissioner, it is hardly likely that personal considerations will step in, and we may, therefore, look to his admirably filling the post to which he is assigned. It is curious to reflect that he takes a post under a Conservative Government, but let us at once say that it is of a kind which does not in any sense involve his going over to the Tories. Assuming that the dispute as to the , Canadian fisheries should still be under con- sideration when Lord SALISBURY'S Adminis- tration is overthrown—a supposition by no means extravagant—Mr. CHAMBERLAIN would nevertheless retain his post, and it is a mat- I ter of course to say that there would be no Idisposition on the part of a new Government to cancel his appointment. The member for West Birmingham is doubtless glad of having the opportunity of getting away just now from English politics ; and almost every section of politicians will feel equally glad to be rid of him for a time. It must be very uncomfortable for Lord HARTINGFON to have a follower at his heels who feels that he ought to be the leader, and who goes his own and another way whenever he thinks fit. On the other hand, the Tories will be by no means miserable at parting with a. " supporter" who has the heart to vote against them in such a critical division as that of Saturday morning last. So far as the Liberal party is concerned, Mr. CHAMBER- LAIN having been a thorn in its side since the failure of the Round Table Conference, there will be a feeling that his going away is, under the circumstances, the best thing that could happen. From every point of view, it may therefore be said that in accepting the appnint- ment of chief Commissioner, Mr. CHAMBER- LAIN will leave his country for his country's good.

"TOUCH AND GO."
On Tuesday night a heavy westerly gale. with copious rain, severely damaged the hops in mid-Kent. Another case, it seems, of being "caught on the hop."

Prince Bismarck has been weighed. He turns the scales'at 207 lbs.—just as he did last year. The man of blood and iron has for a great many years been a man of weight. Pranzini, the triple murderer, was executed in Paris on Wednesday morning. The French still cling to the guillotine, and cut off the heads of their victims. They keep literally to the old text—blood for blood.

The "Daily News" says : " There is to be a great beer exhibition in France, and the "Cologne Gizette" seems to think that there ' ought soon to be one in Germany." In England there is a daily exhibition—not of beer, but of the victims of beer—in the police courts.

There has been a strike at Blackburn in connection with the practic of turning steam into weaving sheds. ThT steam assists the weaver by softening stiff yarn, but, not- withstanding this, the practice is a bad one, for it brings in its train bronchitis, rheuma- tism, and premature death.

On Wednesday, a Liverpool confectioner named Toby, was fined ss and costs for sel- ling adulterated sweetmeats. The sweetmeat —choice meat truly—consisted of " chewing gum," which, on analysis, was found to con- tain 38 per cent, of solid paraffin. nee stuff for children to chew ! Parents should have an eye to this.

Sir Henry Havelock Allen, speaking at a conference of Dissentient Libetals, at Darlington, on Tuesdlv, said, in refer- ence to Mr. Gladstone, that " the idol they formerly followed had been shat- tered." Sir Henry's remark is an idle one ; judging from recent electtons the shattering is all on the other side.

North Hunts has done well. The Tory candidate has been returned, but with a re• duced majority. The Liberals have polled four more and the Conservatives 75 less than at the last election. If the Tories thus con- tinue to lose at bve-elections they cannot win at the next General Election. "There's a good time coming, boys, wait a little longer."

Widnes seems to be earning an unenviable notoriety for deeds of violence. Three pri- soners were committed for trial, on Monday, upon charges of wounding. Mr. Gossage remarked that such cases were more preva- lent in Widnes than formerly. How is this? Can it be that some of the inhabi- tants have taken to drinking rather than thinking?

The shareholders of the Manchester Ship Canal Company behaved badly to Mr. Daniel Adamson at the meeting on Mon- day. The humblest member has a right to be heard without incessant interruption; but to howl down a man who has borne the heat and burden of the day in promoting the schem was utterly discreditable. Mr. Adamson may be in the wrong, but it is no answer to him to howl at him.

During the past year, fir lives have been lost at railway crossings. It is time that the Legislature put an end to these death traps. Railway travelling, it is satisfactory to note, becomes safer year by year. The chances of being killed on an average jouiney are now r 08,000,000 to one. Such long odds open one's eyes to the profitable nature of the business carried on by the Railway Passen- gers' Assurance Company.

Writing in reference to the proposed per- manent arbitration treaty between England and the United States, Mr. Bright expresses himself strongly in favour of it. He says : "England and the States will remain two nations, but I would have them always regarded by themselves as one people." This has the right ring with it; it is like the John Bright of old; but the Tories who ' praise him for his opposition to Home Rule will scoff his peace sentiments.

Typhoid fever is prevalent at Runcorn, and it is stated that one of the docks is in a "very foul state," and has not been cleaned for a quarter of a century. At Weston Point, too, there has been a fatal case of typhoid fever, anent which the opinion is expressed that it has been caused by "the digging up of certain refuse, and inhaling the foul odours of the same." When will people learn that the laws Df health must be observed, if health would be preserved ? Foul smells are the parents of fevers, and fevers are the play- things of the Man with the Scythe.

"A Loyal Catholic" boils over in a con- temporary at the idea of "the. League Hall, in Bewsey-street, Warrington." being lent by the Catholic clergy for a Home Rule meet- ing, when it has hitherto been "associated with the advancement of education and religion." Poor fellow 1 he seems to be hurt inwardly; but it will perhaps tend to- wards his recovery to inform him that the complaint from which he suffers is an imagintry one. The League Hall at which the Home Rule meeting was held was the one in Orford-street--not Bewsey-street.

Mr. John Pierpoint, J.P., was called on ' Alonday, as architect, to give evidence on the plans for the new public-houses which Messrs. Greenall, Whitley, and Co. proposed to build at Warrington, in case new licenses were granted them. The Licensing Corn: mittee refused the applications, but this was not the fault of Mr. Pierpoint. It is stated that he did what he could in the way of moral suasion to influence his brother magis- trates to grant the licenses. Seeing that he was not wholly disinterested, it is being commonly remarked that it would have looked better of him if he had not taken sides. Neutrality is a virtue—sometimes.

The current part of the new edition of the History of Lancashire, published by Mr. John Heywood, is of more than ordinary in- terest. It gives a full account of the part Lancashire played in the history of the coun- tty from the revolution of Charles 11. to the overthrow of the Pretender in 1746. Amongst the list of the ejected members who refused to subscribe to the Act of Uniformity passed in 166 z, we find the following con- nected with this district :—Rev. Thomas Crompton, Astley Chapel, Leigh ; Rev. Jas. Wood. Ashton in-Makerfield ; Rev. John Wright, M.A., Billinge ; Rev. Samuel Mather, M.A., Burton Wood; Rev. William Bell, vicar ol Huyton ; Rev. Thomas Gregg, St. Helens Chapel; Rev. Robert Yates. rector lof Warrington; Rev. Charles Hotham, rector of Wigan.

- I ORDINATION OF PRIESTS AT DITION.-000 Of the most impressive ceremonies in the Catholic Church is the ordina- tion of priests. The Catholic Lord Bishop of Liverpool (the Right Rev. Bernard O'Reilly) c mductednne of these online- Cons in S. Michael's Church, !Anon, on Sunday morning. The candidates for ordination were Bartholomew Omeiner, Christian Blankemeier, Francis Xavier Broahl, Fraucis Xavier than, Francis Xavier Oehry, James Linde°, John Baptist Zonneir, Joseph chmidt, Anthony Weber, Bernard Leiiz. George liurkard. Joseph Haas, and Staoislae Boswin. The Bishop was assisted in his sacred duty by the Father Rectnr of the College (the Rev. Charles Wiedenmann).who acted as archdeacon, and the Rev.. Father Aloysins Steil- brink, Reginald Romanini, and Joseph Amstad, masters of ceremony. The mass for the day was gone through. the organist being the Rev. Father Augustin Martin. During the litany the candidates for ordination prostrated themselves near to the Bishop's faldstool, or throne,and then they knelt two by two at his feet, and received his blessing, and the blessing of the attendants. At the conclusion of the cere- mony the Bishop placed each of the newly-erclained priests upon his throne, and kissed their right hands. Large num- bers of people witnessed the solemn ceremony. Linaker (deputy clerk.)—The Clerk reported that eleven replies had been received to the circular cent out with respect to the Weaver Trust. A. resolution to the following effect had been passed by the Board :—" That the Clerk communicate with the following public lbodies in the county of Chester: Corporations, Improvement Commissioners, Local Boards, Boards of Guardians, and Highway Boards, calling atten- tion to the self-elected representatives on the Weaver Trust, with a view to devising some scheme by which the Weaver will be managed by a body of trustees elected by the rate- payers of the county." About fifty public bodies had been communicated with, but, the Deputy Clerk remarked, none of them seemed to know much about the Trust. Most of those who bad replied asked for further information, and, as the initiative had been taken by that Board he sug- gested that a committtee be appointed to prepare some statement of the facts of the matter.—After a short discus- sion it waS decided to adjourn the matter for a fortnight in order that more replies might be received.—The Board then proceeded to relief butinesse. JDRIREE TREAT TO OLD PEOPLE AT FARNWORTIT.— The Queen's Jubilee was celebrated at Farnworth on Satur- day afternoon and evening by the provision of a tea and entertainment to the elderly people of the parish, no matter of what denomination. The committee who have had charge of collecting subecriptions and finding out the aged people who were privileged to attend, consisted of the following persons :—Mesdames Bond, Haddock, Barlow, Lewis, P Longton, Kershaw, and Hurter, and the 'Misses Hibbert, Bond, Fogg, Bradshaw, M Lea, and Drake. The secretary and treasurer have been the Rev J E Ltwton (curate of the parish) and Mr Robert Kidd respectively, the parties with whom the happy idea originated. Over £2O Was collected, and the 150 or 180 of old ladies and gentle• men who were present were regaled with bounteous store. Their ages ranged from 60 to 86, the person who had seen these many years being an old gentleman in the Shams Cross district. The treat took place in the National School, which had beee neatly decorated for the occasion. The entertainment consisted!of ventriloquial sketches, facial de- lineations, &c., by Mr Roselle, of Liverpool, and songs by Mr J R Lea, Miss Bond, Mr A G Davies, and Mr F Ware- I • mg. At the conclusion each old man was presented with two ounces of tobacco, and each old lady with quarter of a lb. of tea. Carriages and waggonettes were used to bring and take back home these who could not walk. P.C. Messenger described the condition of the woman, And npon..P.C. Davy ent,ring the box to corroborate, the prisoner said "Oh, old Davy will swear anything." (Laughter.) The constable remarked that she struck and kicked him several times, and the greatest difficulty was experienced in conveying her to the police station.—The P,isoner : It's a good job you., have not a black eye. (Laughter.) Ido not know what I was doing to be taken by you. (Renewed laughter.l--The Bench imposed a fine of 10a and costa or in default 14 days' hard lahour, Mr. Goesage remarking that no persons were more sorry to see Mrs Kelly in the ddck than the magis- tht'es —The prisoner called on all the saints to bless the magistrates for their leniency, and declared her intention et going to gaol. _

A RIINOORN GIROCEE IN COI:MT.—At Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, Mr. Edward Johnson, grocer, Bridge- street, and elsuerhere, was charged with having, on the 20th August., at Wearon, delivered bread without providing a pair of scales ear] proper weights for weighing the same.— Mr. Intelsat appeared for the defence --P.C. Breeze de- posed to seeing a man named Thomas Kennedy in charge of a horse and cart, delivering b-cad for the defendant. Kennedy admitted that he had no pules, and refused to supply the officer with a loaf. but ultimately he sold him a 4th loaf for sd.—Cross-examined by Mr. Kitchen, the wit- ness acknowledged that the carter told him that he had not brought the bread for sale; that the bread was bout,ht before. The loaf was weighed in a neighbouring shop, and found to he correct weight.—Mr. Hitchen contended tbat if the officer's evidence was correct, a technical offence had been committed, but his (Mr. Hitchen's) instructions were that the bread was weighed before it was Bent out from the shop, and there was no necessity to carry scales and I weights with bread that was previously o•dered. In his opinion the officer had no ri. ht to demann the loaf, and overstepped his duty in doing so.—Mr. Vincent Johnson stated that the bread was only seat out to cuatomers.— Kennedy, the carter, corroborated.—The magistrates con- sidered the case proved, and imposed a fine of 10a, and costs 12n Bd. _

A CaLtors HUSBAND AT WIDNES.—At Widnes Petty I Sessions, on Thursday, before Messrs Brock and Timm's, a rough looking man, was .broue,ht no on remand charged ' with neglecting to maintain his wife and family in accord- ance with AA order off the magistrates.—Mr. Knowles, solicitor, said the defendant on the 2nd of June promised that he would pay off the arrears of £6 16s 61, at the rate of 101 per week, and also at the same time continue the par- moot of 10s per week under the order. On this under- standing the case was adjourned for three months, but he had not kept his promise, and the arrears now amounted to £6 193 61. Be was employed at a chemiesi works as a charger of revolvers, and earned £2 a week. His wife had Ito keep four children out of 103 per week, whilst he spent 11 his money in drina. Mrs Harrison had to go out charring lin order to prevent herself and children from starving.— The defendant admitted that he was enninz 30s per week, and Mr. Brock said it was quite evident he had made no effort to pay the money. He had set the law at defiance, and thrre was no alternative but to commit him to gaol fott ' a month.—Mr. Lewin informed the defendant that he would clear off the arrears by his imprisonment, hut that be would be liable for the time he was in gami.—Turning to his wife the defendant said " Good bye; bless you for a , month." Noisily stepping from the defendant's box, be , shouted " Put me down below," and expressed a threat that ! he would break the heart of his wife. FARMERS AND THE MILK QITESTION.—A commit- tee meeting of the Warrington Farmers' Club was held at the White Bull, Warrington, on Wednesday, Mr. John Marsh, of Bradley Hall, Grappenhall,in the chair. The Chairman referred to the dismal outlook for dairy farmers in consequence of the dry summer, the scarcity of pasture having caused cows to go off their milk, and necessitated a resort to ex- pensive keep. Northstanding all this, the price of milk remained low, and would continue to do so un- less farmers moved in the matter in a body. The milk dealers in our large towns had their associa- tions, which served them for fixing the price of milk from their point of view, and it was high time that farmers combined wjhi a view of securing a price for their milk more in accordance with the merits of the question. English farmers ;had the whole milk supply in their own hands, and if they could only agree amongst themselves they could easily secure a fair price. lie moved that a special general meeting of the Warrington Farmers! Club be held next Wednesday, 7th September, 1887, at 4_30 p.m., which should constitute itself into a general conference to consider the price of milk, to which all farmers 'should be cordially invited whether members of the club or not. This was seconded, and carried unanimously. -

NEnea. or Tam UT% Mn. Toomm—The remains of the late Mr. William Tootell, of the Crown and Anchor Hotel, Northwich, were in- terred at Warrington Cemetery on Saturday. A deputation from the Gladstone Liberal Club and a number of tradesmen followed the cortege in pro- cession for some distance, leaving Northwich about half-past ten. The cemetery was reached about one o'clock. As a mark of respect tothe memory of the deceased gentleman, most of the residents of High-street and Witton-street lowered their blinds, and several old friends met the funeral party at the cemetery.

PREVENTED FROM COMMITTING SITICIDE. A middle-aged married woman, residing in Isradlegh- road, Earlestown, left her house early on Saturday, and when her daughter came downstairs she found a note written by her mother, to the effect that her husband had done wrong to her, but she would forgive him. It continued, "He will find me in the canal." The girl awoke her father, who proceeded in the direction of the canal. On the way he met his wife being brought back by Mrs Xilshaw, of Bleak House, who, seeing her near the canal, and suspecting that all was not right, went to her. The woman, it is stated, informed Mrs Kilshaw that she intended to drown herself, but she was prevailed upon to desist from her intention. The woman re- turned borne with her husband.

ROYAL LIVER FRIENDLY SOCIETY.—In our ad- uertising columns there will be found some impor- tant extracts from the 37th Annual Report of the Royal Liver Friendly Society, from which it appears that the Reform Management is taking every care to see that the funds are invested in the best securi- ties. Indeed, the list of investments amounting to over .£BOO,OOO shows this. There has been an in- crease on the Benefit Funds of £31,011 Is 30, while the income for 1886 amounted to the large total of .C 402,718 14s 40. Up to the present time over four millions sterling have been paid to mem- bers in claims and grants. Taking everything into account the Committee of Management are well justified in saying "that notwithstanding the agitation the society has passed through, continued and increased prosperity attends the institution." ECCLESTON HALL ESTATE IN TILE MARKET.—An estate well known.not only in this locality, but throughout Lancashire, was offered for sale at the Law Association Rooms, Liverpool, by Messrs. J. B. and B. Leach, on Tuesday. The event excited considerable notice among those interested in landed and other property in this part of the coun- try, and the proceedings Indicated the great change which has recently taken place in the value of estates of this description. The property offered far sale was well known, and although its disposal was extensively advertised there was only a moderate attendance. It is situated in the town- ship of Eccleston, about midway between the towns 01St. Helens and Prescot, and within eight miles of Liverpool, and comprises the family mansion .of Eccleston Hall, with its gardens, pleasure grounds, park, drives, and plantations; seven farms, vary- ing in size from 25 to 115 acres, with well-built homesteads, a corn mill, and smith's and wheel- wright's shop, a licensed inn, known as "The Griffin Inn," and several lodges and cottages ; ex- tensive reservoirs, valuable mines of coal, stone quarries, and beds of 'nick and pottery clay. The property contains numerous and eligible building sites, with frontages of nearly five miles to public highways, and forms an estate of seven hundred and sixty-one acres. The sale included several leasehold and perpetual rents, also the lordship of the manor, or reputed manor, of Eccleston, and the perpetual right of presentation to the• living of Christ Church, Eccleston. In opening the sale, Mr. J. B. Leach said it seldom fell to the lot of an auctioneer to be honoured with instruct;ons to sell such valuable property as that before them, and he drew attention to the many special advantages of an investment of that kind. They admitted that an agricultural depression existed in the country, but this estate was one of those which stood aloof from such depression. It was said the income from the estate was not very large, but it was only partly developed. By a judicious laying out of the • boundaries as a residential estate, and without in- juring the dimensions of the farm, a very large 'rental coUld be realised. Th 6 resources of the estate were not by any means touched yet. Eccleston Hall was in splendid order, and the farms were laid out, occupied, and cultivated in good style. He then invited off- rs, and after considerable hesitation £60,000 was offered, followed by .£65,000, but as there was no advance on this figure the property was withdrawn.

THE DROWNING FATALITY AT WIDNES : THE
DEPUTY CORONER ON D 'Eti.N K".

The Deputy Coroner (Mr. W. T. Husband), on Saturday held an inquest at the West Bank Hotel, respecting the death of Richard Eaton, 27 years of age, who was captain of the flit Prima Donna, of Winsford. Thos. Eaton, of Leicester-street. Nordawich, identified the .body as that of his eon, and Joseph Warourton, of 12, Slensey-road, and foreman at the Widnes dock, deposed that on Thursday night be and the eleceoed were together at the Swan Inn. Waterloo-road, from six o'clock to eleven o'clock. When they left deceased was not drunk, but he was not in a fit state to go home himself and witness went with him to his flat. Deceased, however, walked along the rough, uneven road without assistance Witness ease him go upon rho deck of the boat and walk towards the cabin. He asked the deceased if he was all right, and he replied "Yes, all right," and wituess then left. Ile did not see the deceased co into the cabin, for, as a rule, sailors pulled their boots off before entering the cabin, and witness thodght the deceaspd was going to pull his boots off because he stooped. He had since been told by the mate that there was nobody on the flat, and in that case the deceased would not able to get into the cabin, and would probably sleep on deck.—ln reply to questions, the witness said he did not think the deceased had thrown himself into the water. While they were in the Swan Inn they had each four or live glasses of beer and porter mixed. He could see that the deceased wasa little the worse for drink, and pre- vented himltem havisn,, a greater quantity. He tried to persuade him to go home. One of the Waitresses eerved them. Anyone could see that the deceased had had drink, but he was not drunk.—Thomas Fletcher, of Hartford-road, Davenham, captain of the flat Two Sisters, stated he grappled and recovered the body of the deceased from the dock.—The Deputy Coroner, in summing up, said tiv evi- dence was rather scant upon the very point upon which it was most r(quired—the way in Which the dec,as,(l got into the canal. The probability was, considering his state, and the fact that the cabin was fastened, that he fell asieeu on deck and rolled into the water. If the jury were (ado to come to a verdict that day he would suggest that they should return an open one. If they wished to make any i reference as to the state the deceased was n they were at liberty to do so, but as the action of himself and a jary with reatel to A man killed at Messrs. rtlicanzton's works had recently been called in question by a correepon lont of a newspaper, he would advise them not to say anything re- specting drink without due consideration. He did not wish to influence them, but there was no (direct evidence in this case as there was in the one referred to that death had come from the effects of drink. The writer of tho letter referred to, he presumed, was an embusiafdic teetotaller, And neu. doubt was acting for the good of what be called the cans e. but probably a verdict having any reference to drink Ivo, id do more injury to the relations of the deceased tha n it would benefit the temperance eause.—The jury return(' i an open verdict, and made no reference to think..

BOLTON STRIKE.—The engineers' strike at Bolton is, we regret to say, apparently no nearer a settlement now, after lasting sixteen weeks, than at any time since the commence - melt. A circular issued on Thursday by the workmen asserts emphatically that the employers are responsible for the strike, and that the men are only seeking the return of the wages taken from them in March of last year. A pro- posal to create a co-operative ironworkers' society " has been discussed by representatives from the Strike Commit- tee, the District Co-operative Association, and the Bolton Trades' Council. but so far without definite result. It was stated at a meeting of the Trades' Council that labour can., didates will, if necessary, contest all seats in the Town Council becoming vacant in November next.

WARIONOTON V BIRKENHEAD PARK (2ND ELEVENS.) —This match was played on the Arpley Ground on Satur- day, and resulted in a win for the home team. At 6-35 the visitors had scored 80 for the loss of five wickets, only leaving 25 minutes for the home team to make a win in; but by the excellent bowling of the Brothers Hind, and the smart Fielding of the team in general, the last wicket fell at 6-55 for the small total of 96, only leaving five minutes to the time appointed for the withdrawal of stumps. H Jolley, C Unswerth, and J Wignell played excellent cricket for their respective scores. div.p: NOTES BY THE WAY.

The Lancashire cricket season was brought to a close on Tuesday with a one innings victory over Northampton- shire. In all Lancashire have won 16 matches, lost three, and drawn two, having twice beaten Sussex, Kent, Derby- shire, Gloucestershire, Northamptonshire, and Cheshire, while with Nottingham and Surrey they have won one and lost one. Against Yorkshire they fared badly, the first con- test being drawn very much against them, and in the re- turn game played at Old Trafford, they suffered a severe re- verse. The matches with Oxford University terminated in a draw and a win both in favour of Lancashire; while the engagement with the Marylebone Club and Ground, resulted it will be remembered, after an exciting finish, in a victory for Lancashire by two wickets. Mr. 9. G. Steel heads the list in the batting averages with 68.1, bathe is undoubtedly in a false position having only played in two innings. Rob- inson, who has played in nearly all the matches, is really first with 3419. Mr. J. Eccles closely follows Robinson with 33.17. Mr. A N Ilornby has played twp or three good innings, but his average of 284 in 23 completed in- nings does not come up to expectation. F Sugg, the ex- Derbyshire professional, has shown excellent form. Briggs, we should liked to have seen higher up the list, bat his duties during the season have been exceptionally heavy, and his averages in both batting and bowling do him great credit. He has lost none of his dash in the field, and the applause which has greeted his efforts in that line has been great. The Yorkshiremen on Satarday finished a singularly un- equal season. At times they showed form equal to that of any county in England, and at other times they played very, disappolating cricket. They beat Derbyshire twice, anti Kent, Sussex, Gloucestershire, and Lancashire once each. They were twice beaten by Surrey and once by Middlesex, while the drawn games were against Notts twice, Glouces- tershire, Kent, Lancashire, Middlesex, and Suesex. Below is a table giving the total number of first-class county matches playcd, with the results of them all and jibe Clubs in order of merit. Fifty-seven county matches have been played, of which all but fourteen were brought to a definite conclusion. surrey must be regarded as the premier or champion county of the year, and Lancashire runs a very good second : Matches played. THE COST OF LUNATICS. A short conversation took place as to the comparative cost of maintaining pauper lunatics at the different asylums, to which they were sent, and it was mentioned that the cost at Ittinhil/ exceeded that of other asylums. An opinion was- expressed by several members that lunatics should be sent, when practicable, to the asylums at which the cost of Maintaining them was least. Ilia was all the business of public interest.

A correspondent who signs himself " D" in the "Journal of Horticulture and Cottage Gardener," gives the following account of a visit to Councillor Bolton, of Warrington : • Amongst those northern amateurs who have made their mark as successful growers and raisers of auriculas, not only did he this year carry off the Turner Memorial prize, but he also gained other prizes, and exhibited and obtained prizes for seed- lings of his own raising, and I therefore think that notes of a visit I paid to him the other day may not be uninteresting, especially as not only did I see his, collection, but also had a talk with him on various I matters connected with our favourite flower, and may thus perhaps meet the wants of your corres- pondent in a recent number of the journal. Mr. Bolton's collection I have known and seen the progress of for some years. When I first saw it it was a small one, and was contained in a small house In a backyard in Mersey-street, Warrington. When I next saw it it was in Latchford-road, a little way out of the town, and now he has removed to Stockton Heath, about two miles off, where, in purer air, and with larger surroundings, he is able to carry out not only his love for this flower, but also for other things connected with horticulture. One can always learn something, even in unlooked for ways, if we keep our eyes open, and so here I saw, for the first time, the sweet-scented and pretty Cape efondweed (Aponoueton distachyon) grown in pans in a greenhouse. °The house being badly ventilated, Mr. Bolton had put in several large pans of it, about 18 inches across, in order that they might give out some moisture by evapor- ation, so as to take away from the excessive dry- ness of the atmosphere. They answered a twofold purpose, for they were in flower all the winter, and supplied him plenty of cut blooms. But to return to the auricula. Mr. Bolton has considerably increased his collection, but so far as named sorts are concerned, it is nothing like as large as many collections I have seen (Mr. Wood- hea I's for example), for like most of those who grow seedlings, he gives mme attention to them, and believes he will raise some that will surpass those we already have. With regard to potting. Mr. Bolton thinks-that , it is a mistake to repot before July. His idea is, I that after the plants have done flowering,they com- mence rapidly to form the plant for the following year, and that the heart then fills up with the new growth. If they are repotted, then this growth is checked, and that, therefore, it is better to wait un- til July, when, if repotted, the plants will begin to push roots, especially about the centre of the plant, where he is more anxious that it should be done, instead of pushing out to the sides of the pot. He uses glazed pots, as they necessitate less water- ing, and are more easily kept clean, so that the I sneers with which some meet the use of glazed pots as opposed to all scientific theories, only shows that practice is a good deal better than theory in many cases, and in this amongst the number. Like many successful growers he has given up the old- fashioned practice of top-dressing, which used to be considered one of the most essential and important parts of auricula culture. Like most growers, too, he has discarded all the nostrums wherewith the poor plants used to be physicked in former days, i and altogether I feel that the older race of florists have been considerably taken down in these days; the older varieties have given way to newer ones; the old practices have been abandoned, and simpli- city has become more the character of Auricula cul- I ture. In potting he believes in potting firmly, and ' in placing some material over the broken potsherds, so as to prevent the soil being washed down into the drainage—moss, spent hops, the more fibrous pieces of the loam, are all useful for this pur- pose—in fact anything that will keep the drainage clear.

With regard to that nuisance to the Auricula grower, autumnal blooming, he does not think that the time of repotting makes any difference what- ever in its frequency or otherwise, lie believes it to belong to particular varieties, and do what you will, some of them will bloom in the autumn; but he says that if the bloom is nipped off as soon as it ap- pears, the plant, if vigorous, will bloom again in the spring, and he mentioned one case of a plant that had done so, which was one of his winning flowers this year. There seems to me to be reason in this, and it may thus comfort those who are troubled by it.

In repotting, Mr. Bolton is careful to look after the tap roots of the better and scarcer varieties. I All Auricula growers know that the main root of the Auricula runs down and forms a large central root or carrot, which is oftentimes the cause of dis- ease and loss, but it will often be found that there I are incipient shoots which are the precursors of offsets if properly treated. His plan is to cut this off, leaving a sufficient number of healthy roots for the nourishment of the plant. The tap is then planted in a small pot, and a bellglass placed over it. This induces the shoots to push oat, and in the ' course of a little while they will show themselves as offsets. When rooted they should be taken off, and planted round the edge of a pot, when they will speedily increase in size. Mr. Bolton is, as I have said, engaged in raising seedlings, and a considerable number of these were planted out in a bed in the garden. They are planted there as soon as they are fit to handle, and as they increase in size, if they show any good properties, are lifted up and potted. In the green- , house were to be seen some pans where the seed- lings were coming up very thickly, but his ex- perience, as well as Mr. Homer's, is the same as that which one finds in other flowers, that those which come up quickly are rarely ever worth any- thing. I remember years ago Margottin at Bourg la Reine telling me that he had never found that the rose seedlings which came up the first year pro- duced anything worth retaining. With regard to giving heat to auriculas to bring them on in time for exhibition, he looked upon it as in itself an injurious thing. A good deal of the roughness of many exhibits he attributes to this, and he believes no auricula grower would apply it if he could help it. He is himself preparing to build a house for flowering plants, as, like other growers, he finds it so much preferable to frames, where you can walk in and have the plants at the level of your eye. It will thus be seen that we ranged in our con- versation over most of the subjects connected with auricula culture. Mr. Bolton is one of those who believe that there are no secrets in auricula grow- ing, and that growers can best promote its interestsl by communicating their ideas to one another.

NORTH HUNTS ELECTION,—The result of the voting on Tuesdty in the election of a member for North Huntingdon- shire in the place of Captain Fellowes, who has been called to the House of Lords, was announced on Wednesday as fol- lows :—Fellowes (C), 2,700 •, Sanders (L). 2,4l4—maior- ity, 280. The figures in 1885 were :—Captain Fellowes (C), 2,775 ; Lord D. Gordon (L), 2,410 ; Conservative majority, 385. At the last election Captain Fellowes was returned unopposed, and there are no means of guaging the exact position of the two parties at that time. WARRINGTON BOARD OF

The fortnightly meeting of this Board was held at the Workhouse on Wednesday morning. There were present the Rev. G. F. Roberts (chairman), Messrs. Derbyshire, Harrison, Voisey, Gibson, W. Houghton, Humphreys, Jolley, Bonnet!, Clarke, Eckersley, Grange, John Houghton, Bethany, Jones, Hibbert ; and C Sutton (clerk).

div.head: TN& MIZZEN. OF MR: BROWN.
div.p: TN& MIZZEN. OF MR: BROWN.

In reply to Mr. Harrison, the CLERK said that be had caused inquiries to be made the previous day as to the illness of Mr. Brown' the junior vice-chairman of the Board, and he understood that Mr. Brown was progressing very favour- ably. THE SCHOOLS COMMITTER.—THE DEATH OF MRS. NAYLOR.

The Padgate Schools etammittee in talc n;inlat;s ;;;Cl. that the committee regretted to report the death, on August 26th, at the schools, of Mrs. Naylor, the schoolmistress. They desired to place on record their appreciation of Mrs. Naylor's faithful and efficient services to the Union exT tending over a period of ten years, and to express their sympathy with her husband, the assistant schoolmaster, in his bereavement. Thaeommittee recommended that a cer- tificated schoolmistrese be advertised for on the terms upon which Mrs. Naylor held the appointment. They also reoommended that Mies Humphries be appointed to act as temporary schoolmistress until the appointment of Mrs.. Naylor's successor on the same terms. The Committee hav- ing examined,the applications and testimonials of the can- didates for the office of industrial teacher and mother of home, recommended the appointment of Miss Ann Dearden. of Marton, near Northwich, on the terms advertised.—The. Superirtendent (Mr. Mines) stated in his report book that it I was his painful duty to report the death of Mrs. Naylor, ' their late schoolmistress (on the 26th inst.), who for ten years performed her duties in a mast praiseworthy manner, and with excellent results. Ho might add that it was touching to witness the emotion of the children on hearing of Mrs. Naylor's death, their erpressions of sympathy and regret at the !Gni of an old and valued toacher, and the general conduct of both officers and children under the painful circumstances, had been highly corammadable.—The Cnatumax, in moving the confirmation of the minutes, said the death of Mrs. Naylor was a great shock to him. It was very sudden and very sad, and they sympathised very much with Mr. Naylor in his bereavement. (Hear, hear.)—Mr. CLARKE seconded the adoption of tho minutes, which was agreed to.

The CLERH reporUed that there were now only three townships, viz., Grappenhall, Rixton, and Southworth- with-Croft, in arrears as regarded the payment of tbe calls upon them.—Mr. DARISYSHIRE said he understood that the call upon Grappenhall had bees paid the previous day. He also inquired 143. to who it Watithat 62rsed the date of the calla. He thought it would be better if the dates were fixed nearer the end of tho hal f-year, andtbat would also give more time for collectimg the rate. Ratepayers could not be compelled to pay till the end of the halt..year—The CLERK said thabMr. Derbyshire was in error aa regarded the last statement, as all rates were due upon demand, and the law would cer- tainly enable the overseers to enforce payment. With re- gard to the fixing of the dates of the calls, that resaed with the Guardians. They,, however, never took proceedings for the payment of the calls, provided they had money in the bank to enable them to go on.—The matter then dropped. _

WARRINGTON BREWSTER SESSIONS. The adjourned licensing sessions for the hearing of applications was held at the Court-room in lrlam street, on Monday morning. The members of the Licensing Committee present were The Mayor (Alderman Pickmere), Aldermen Holmes, Davies, and Harrison, Councillors Greening and Francomb, and Mr. John Fairclough. The following members of the Borough Bench were also present :—Messrs. E. J. Guest, R. Garnett, T. Litton, John Burgess, Thomas Sutton, and F. Monks. Amongst those in court, which was crowded, were the Revs. J. J. Langham, G. D. Wray, G. E. Young, G. E. Cutting, J. 11. Jones, F. L. Good, J. Warnock, and Edward Moore. Mr. Ridgway, solicitor, was present on be- half of the Warrington Temperance Federation.

MESSRS. ORZENALL'S APPLICANIONS. Mr. Robert Davies, on behalf of Messrs. Greenall, Whit- ley, and Co., brewers, applied for a provisional victuallers' license for premises proposed to be erected in Hoyle-street, off Bewsey-road. In effect, however, he said his application was only for a transfer.—Mr. Ridgway said that on behalf of the Warrington 'Temperance Federation he wished to present petitions against the granting of any new licence. There was also a letter addressed to the Mayor from the Rector of Warrington.—Mr. Davies said he should okject to private letters being handed to the Bench to be read, as he did not think that was a matter at all within the powers of magistrates. At Salford, where no doubt they had the best advice, memorials were objected to. and the magi- strates' clerk advised the magistrates that they were illegal and could not be received. He had no wish to shut an, - one's mouth, because if he could not convince the Bench that the application he was about to make was deeirable, it would be refused. He thought they ought to know what people wished to say from their own mouths or by their properly•constituted representatives. He must certainly object to any letter being received by the Bench ; at all events to influence them in their decision.—The Mayor said he had had several letters addressed to him on various matters by complainanta and defendants, anl on all Occa- sions had declined to open or read them till the case was decilad.—Mr. Davies said it was hardly within the province

of magistrates to argue the question of principle whether licences were desirable or not. A teetotaller would con- scientiously oppose the granting of every licence through- out the town, but the trade had been sanctioned by the Legislature, and the magistrates sat there to administer the law, and net to take the opinion of one section of the community, however numerous it might be. fie should therefore object on principle to rnemotials being put in, but any witness could be heard by the Bench as ratepayers.— The Clerk: An association can have no locus standi except as ratepayers.—Mr. Ridgway said one of the petition* was that practically of the whole of the clergy of all denomi- no tions in the Borough. If the Bench would not receive the petitions, then the course he should have to take would be to put the rev, gentlemen in the box to state their feelings in the matter.— The Mayor intimated that they were advised that they had no right to receive the petitions.—Mr. Davies then pro- ceeded to say that Messrs. Greenall, Whitley, and Com- pany had for years desired to alter many of their old houses in Warrington, for which they had had licenses possibly for the best part of a century, the accommodation being inade- quate for the wants of a town like Wartington. They did not wish to increase the number of licenses, but in the two applications he was instructed to make he offered in one case a lull licensed house and a beerbouse, and in the other case a full license and two off-licenses, which, in his opinion, did more mischief than licensed houses under the supervision of the police. Licensed victuellere' houses were houses of accommodation, where scores of visitors to tome sleep at night. It was proposed to give up houses situated in an objectionable position—one, the Green Dragon, off Bridge-street, and another the Fox, which was getting an old house—and to build others in localities which had been chosen for them. One of the houses would coot £2,500, and the other, with a bowling green, something like £2,700. They knew that the whole licensing system wanted taking in hand, but if they were to argue the matter on teetotal grounds he did not know where the matter would end. It was quite evident they would not agree. It was both to Conservative and to Liberal Govern- meets that they owed an extension of the licensing busi- ness. It was to a Liberal Government they owed the off licenses, he believed, although he was not talking politically. He meant to say that these things had been put on to raise money, and all parties seemed to be alike in extending the facilities for drinking. Lie recollected Warrington when it had a population of 18,000 persons, and at the present time it amounted to something like 48,000, and the population was increasing at the rate of a thousand a year. He saw statements made occasionally that there was a certain amount of drunkenness on the part of females, but if so it might be because they got better wages than were received in most places. He was going to state a startling fact to the Bench. Warrington once had a population of 18,000, and, with the exception of one or two licenses, no full license had been granted for many years, except at the rail- way stations. The old houses, suitable for old days, still re- mained, although the population was increasing, and the ' question was whether the Bench would distribute the houses • or whether they would keep them crammed three or four in a street, or enable good houses to be built. Mr. Davies then read a statement showing the number of licensed premises as compared with population, in the twelve towns men- tioned:— Blackburn, lin 216 ; Manchester, lin 214; Al- trincharn, lin 211; Hyde, 1 in 203 ; Preston, 1 in 199; Stockport, lin 19 - ; Knutsford, lin 189 ; Rochdale, 1 in 181 ; Wigan, lin 177 ; Blackpool, 1 in 155; Salford, 1 in • 169; Warrington, lin 237." The magistrates had no right to take licenses away, and the question was whether they would allow his clients to buila good hotels, with ample ac- commodation, in place of the old houses. His belief was that the habits of the people would improve, and he did not think he was asking them to do anything which would in- crease drunkenness in Warrington. He proposed to do away with five licenses and to take two, giving three to be abol- • ished—the Green Dragon, the Fox, and the White Bear beerhouse—and two off licenses off Bewsey-road.—Mr John • Pierpoint, architect, prodaced plans of the preposed hotel, 1 and stated that the nearest licensed house would be the Three Pigeons Inn, which was 960 yards away and the next the Cooper's Arms, which was distant 1,150 yards. There , was a beerhouse 250 or 300 yards away. The ,estimated cost would be about £2,600, He knew that it was proposed • to build a Mission Hall 200 yards away, in connection with St. Paul's Church.

Mr. Davies then applied for a license in respect to the lime proposed to be built in Bittersby•lane. In cases where a public-house was properly conducted the proprietor must not be ostracised for carrying on a business which, though capable of abuse in certain respects, was essentially necessary. Everyone knew the amount of business that was done in public-houses, and there was not one of them who went to a town on business who was not compelled to use an inn or a public-house according to his station. The general public, as a rule, did not go to temperance houses, and the magistrates must, therefore, consider the population with which they had to deal. Referring to the police cases which had been heard that morning, Mr. Davies remarked that only two or three persons had been brought up on a charge of drunkenness, but a bad lot of people had been brought before the Bench, whose convictiens were frequent.. It might be that if no one took any stimulants the world would be better off than it was at the present moment, but he was afraid it was hardly ripe for that state of things yet, and they must legislate as they found things.—. Mr. John Pierpoint produced the plaes of the proposed house. Tee next house was 430 yards away, namely, the Glassmakere Arms; in Crosley-street, and that was a beerhouse. The nearest fully licensed house was the Manx Arms, on School- brow, the distance being NO yards.—Mr. Ridgway.—How far is the proposed house from 'the house occupied by Mr. Henry Merte, on whose behalf an application is to be made here to-day.--Mr. Pierpoint replied that he could not tell. —Mr. Arthur Browne : Ten yards.—Mr. F. Monks : Have you ascertained the number of off-beerhouses ?—Mr. Pier- point : I have not taken that matter into consideration at all.—Mr. Monks : Because from the return we have before us there are twenty.—Mr. Pierpoint: No doubt there are too maim—Mr. Monks: I have nothing more to say ; I have simply to point out the fact.—Mr. Pierpoint said be estimated that the cost of the house would be, including the stables, about £2,500.

THE GROVE, REWSET-ROAD. Mr Mulholland, barrister, made application OD behalf of Mr Elijah Lawton for a full alehouse licence for the Grove, Bewsey-road, which has now an off-licence. He was not present, he said,to make an application merely on plans, nor did he apply to the Bench on behalf of any brewer, but he tendered to the Bench a gentleman whose character I would be Investigated, and the already existing house would be made into a house of first-class accommodation to the I neighbourhood. He found that Mr Davies' application was on behalf of the manager of a large brewery concern, known as "Messrs Greenall, Whitley, and Co." He contended that it was necessary that the applicant should attend him- self. The Bench must see the applicant to whom it was proposed that the licence should be given. His absence ap- peared to him to be a fatal objection to the application by Mr Davies. He (Mr Mulholland) claimed for a house which was already in existence. It was purchased for £4,000 from the late owner, and it was now intended to spend £1,200 upon it. There was already a bowling green attached, and ample stable accommodation. It was not his intention to sum up the whole of Warrington, and find how many houses there were; his contention was that in this neigh- bourhood, the population of which was rapidly increasing there were a number of men who had very exhausting and, arduous labours to perform, and there was absolutely no place where a glass of brandy could be e,btained in case of accident or illness. The only place where a glass of beer could be obtained was the little beethwase in Pitt-street. There was DO other house until they came to the, Three Pideons, 650 yards off, and the Horse and Jockey was 1,500 yards away. His client was the first in the field, the beer- house licence having been in existence for eleven years, while the applicant had been in charge of tbe house for the last nine years; and he contended that if any fairness was to prevail between one applicant and another, at all events his client should have the preference.—Mr Robert Davies remarked that the licences were applied for by the Brewery Company itself. The present was precisely the form of notice which he got in the case of the Saracen's Head at Wilderspool, which was pulled down for the accommoda- tion of the Brewery Company, and it was held that as they were to build the house they were the parties who had to give the notice Mr. Mulholland : The company cannot apply for a licence. Mr. Davies: Then that would mean a company cannot build a new house at all.—Mr. Mulholland said that the

application should be made in the name of a particular Person, who could he fined if he ccrnmitted or allowed a breach), of the law to take place.—Mr. James Adams, archi- tect, produced plans of the premises as it was proposed to alter them.—The Mayor : This seems to be a new erection; the front is practically new.—Mr. Ridgway : Who are the *mime cf the house ?—Mr. Adams : Messrs Wagstaffe at d Co., of Manchester.—Mr. Ridgway : They are a large firm of brewers. You are practically going to erect a huge struc- ture 7—Mr. Adams :It will be a first-class, decent-sin d hotel.—Mr. Ridgway : And if the licenses are granted there will be two big houses in that district. A little rivalry be- tween two large brewers.—Mr. Elijah Lawton was then ex- amined as the applicant. He had sold for the last nine years wiah an off-license at the Grove. lie was well ac- quainted with the neighbourhood. There was a want of a respectable house in the neighbourhood where men could have beer. A great number of men came to the house every day, took out their beer and sat in the &Id adjoining the house to drink it. Some days he had seen from 50 to 60 persons thus engaged. Be bad no control over them, but he would have if they were in the house. It was a usual occur- rence in fine weather to see men drinking in the field. There was a beerhouse in Pitt-street, but it was a small one. Some of the men who signed the petition in his favour said that if the license were granted it would save them many' pounds in the course of the year, as when they went to town they did not know when they would come back.—Mr. Ridgway said that as far as accidents at the works were concerned a supply of brandy was kept there.---The Appli- cant : Yes, but the men never get any. They keep it in the office where the clerks are. (Laughter.) There was one poor man fell a few months ago through exhaustion. No one has asked me for accommodation for the night during the last twelve months. ANOTHER PROPOSED HOTEL FOR BATTERSBY-LANE. Mr. Arthur Browne applied for a full ale-house license on behalf of Mr. Henry Morte, of Battersby-lane, an if license holder. His client came before the Beech as a householder, and as an outdoor beerhouse keeper in Batt. rsby-lane. They did not propose to provide any commercial, room for Battersby-lane, because they did not expect to see any com- mercials in it; but they proposed to erect a plain building suitable for the neighbourhood; what was required WAS a place that would :nit classes who lived in the (Beirut, and who were principally employed at the Cheshire Lines works. The house belonged to Councillor Bolton. —Mr. J. E. Wright produced the plans, and pointed out that the population of the district was increasing rapidly. There was no beerhouse in the neighbour- hood, and Bittersby-lane was on the way to the barracks.— In answer to Mr. Ridgway, Mr. Wright said he believed there was a canteen at the barracks for the convenience of the soldiers.—Mr. R dgway then addressed the B,nch in opposition to the granting of any license. As far as the two houses were concerned for which Mr. Davies hid beer) applying he felt in a great difficulty, because the learned counsel had pointed out that application had been m.,de for a bou-e although there was no applicant to shoot at, whereas Mr. Mulholland and Mr. Browne had put their cliems in the box and bad thus treated him fairly. What were the appli- cations before the court 7 Practically for four houses, and In respect of two Mr. Davies appeared. The very applica- tions themselves showed the Bench that if they granted one all should be granted, and that the fairest way to deal with the matter would be to refuse the whole of the applications. Messrs. Greenall and Co. applied for new houses, and Messrs. Wagstaffe and Co., a large firm of brewers in Man- chester, for a full alehouse license, whilst Mr. Browne made another and a similar application. The real applicents were all brewers, and all in business, and neither wished another brewer to have the advantage of getting another heuse. He would serve all alike Mr. Davies had' made a strong point about the giving up of the Fox Inn, the Green Dragon and the White Bear beer- house, and two off-licenses in Boyle street. He could only suppose that the houses proposed to be given up were not doing as much as they ought to do. The idea was to get two large houses put up in fairly prosperous districts, and thus get two good businesses. There was another point, and it was with reference to l'he Grove, the tenant of which bad told tho Bench that the license had been a little bit of trouble to bins, for he had had to watch the men drinking outside. Was it not a pity to saddle him with a greater reseonsibility by giving him more men to look after in his own house ? With reference to the question of brandy or spirits, required in case of need, when it was really wanted it could be obtained at the works —Mr. Davies said a remark had been made to the effect that there bad been no one to shoot at as far as his applications were concerned, but there were persens present in court to represent the brewery. He could only apply for a provisional license by any person interested.—The Licensing Committee retired to consider their decision, and on their return the Mayor said they had decided to refuse all the applications.

man of badreputation was comp aming o his uncle that a certain person had ruined his character. "So much the better," replied the uncle, "for it was a very bad one; and the sooner it was destroyed the more to your advantage." A phrenologist says that the fighting bump is just a little above the ear. sow, this is not always the case, for when a woman is fighting with her husband and lifts up the poker and cracks him behind the head he gene- rally finds his bump rising there. A celebrated doctor arrived at the house of a friend who was expecting him to dinner. "I am completely exhausted," he exclaimed, as he mopped his brow. "My patients are killing me." "Come, doctor," said his friend, "you ought not to complain. It is only a case of just retaliation."

"The nearest I ever came to cannibalism," said the late George Bentinck, "was when I swallowed a little London porter." REMEDY on ROACTIES.—A lady recently asked a painter what was good for roaches. His reply was, "Try meal and sugar, it will fatten them. It has never been known to fail."
HER CRITERION OF EDIJCATION.—Mother : "Flow do you'like Mr. de Snoodle ?" Daughter : "Oh, he's just lovely—such an educated man! I didn't understand half .of what he was talking about." . .
Mistress, to new cook: r" Bridget, the soup is quite cold. Didn't I tell you to warm the tureen ? Bridget: " Yis, mum; but shure an' I thought the soup wud warrum the toorane !"

"Do you think," she asked dreamily, as he sat beside her at the circus, "that this is the same elephant I saw when I was a child ?" "No," he answered, with scornful candour; "you know elephants only live to be two hun- dred years old." She has another beau now. At the library. Lady: "I'm getting tired of modern fiction; can't you recommend me a good exciting standard work ?" Librarian: "Have you read 'The Last Days of Pompeii 9'" Lady: "No, I believe not. Can you tell me what he died of?" Librarian: "An eruption, I believe." It is noted as a singular philological fact, at London, that some of Buffalo Bill's Indians speak the Cherokee language with a strong Irish accent. One of them came very near giving himself away by smoking his pipe up- side down. . _ _

"I regard the use of beer as the true temperance principle. When I work all day and am exhausted, nothing helps me like a glass of beer. It assists nature, you understand," said Benison to Benson. "It makes a fool of me," Benson replied. "Just so," exclaimed Remson—" that's what I say; it assists nature." "Do you know," remarked a rather fast youth the other day to a stuttering friend to whom he was slightly indebted, do you know that I intend to marry and settle down ?" '1 do-don't know anything about it," was the reply, " bu-but I think you had better stay single and set-settle up." A Chinese in America was a witness at an inquest. He was asked how he took an oath. He said, "On the book." The magistrate then asked if he were a Christian. He replied that he was. The magistrate then inquired what he meant by being a Christian. The witness answered, "Oh, wearing a coat like yours, and being a great swell." An Irishman having accidentally broken a pane of glass in a window, was making the best of his way out of sight; but, unfortunately for Pat, the proprietor stole a march on him, and having seized him by the collar, exclaimed, "You broke my window, fellow, did you not ?" To be sure I did, said Pat, "and didn't you see me running home for the money to pay for it ?" "What is more awful to contemplate,' said a lecturer, glaring about him, "than Ihe relentless power of the Maelstrom?" And a hen-pecked looking man in the rear of the building softly replied : " Femalestrom." A witty and attractive young lady asked the following question :—" What is the difference between myself and the clock ?" "Mademoiselle, the clocks tell the hours, and you make us forget them," was the very natural reply." "So you are going to keep a school ?" said a young lady to her old aunt. "Well, for my part, sooner than do that I would marry a widower with nine children." "I should prefer that myself," was the reply; "but where is the widower ?" First Masher: Well, did you make the acquaintance of that strange girl you were raving over ?—Second ditto : Yes, followed her home.—First ii.: How did she strike you ? Second ditto: She didn't at all; she got her big brother to do it.

Ci-LADSTONE'S DINNER TO TUC AGED.—In commem- oration of the Jubilee of Her Majesty's reien the aged peo- ple in the Parish of Hawarden were enterained at dinner on Tuesday afternoon by Mr. and Mrs. Gladstone. In an ad- dress which he delivered Mr. Gladstone contrasted the pre- sent Juhilee with that of George the Third, which was, be said, one of great folks, while the present one was a jubilee of the nation. tie also dwelt upon the various improve- ments which have taken place during the last fifty years in the condition of the working classes. In alluding to the present occupant of he throne Mr. Gladstone said that Her Maj,!sty bad observed all the principli,s of the Constitution more perf‘ctly than any former Sovereign ; in point of fact, it was not too much to say that the historian, when he came to write an account of the period during which the Queen had reigo,d, would point to it as the time in which the Sovereign of this cduntry Caine finally and fully to understand the constitutional position and the great and noble conditions on which a free people should be governed. %ditto to the attn. WARRINGTON INTERCEPTING DEPOTS. Sir,—Because I ventured to say a very few words in de- , fence of these depots, Mr. Diggle charges me with being an interested person. I axis afraid I must plead guilty to this charge. lat once confess that I feel interested in the depots. I look upon them as part 0 a scheme, which, if succkssf al, will confer great material benefits on,Warring- -ton, and place the town in the honourable position of a -pioneer in the noble science of sanitation. As for being "interested" in the depots in any other way, I must digpwn the " soft impeachment." I have no cottages or any other kind of property which wild be affected one way or the other by the depots. • Mr. Diggle predicts that the scheme will "ultimately prove a failure." We all know that Mr. Diggle bee a weakness for prophecy. He is our loc il Cas- sandra, but he is not inspired, and experience has shown that if we reverse his predictions we will get pretty near the mark. His latest attempt to foretell what is to happen in the future must, therefore, be very encouraging to those who wish for the success of the depot scheme.—Yours, drc.. S. M.

THE WARRINGTON LIBRARY. Sir,—l think it must now be regarded as a settled matter that the Library Committee will net merely not do any- thing to promote the freeing of the library, but also that they will throw obstacles in the way of every project that has this object in view. This conclusion is forced upon us by the manner in which the committee kas treated every proposal that has been pat before them by the advocates of a free library. It seems to me, therefore, that something else most be tried. The Town Council is the master of the Committee, and the Council is the creature of the rate- payers. Let the seat of every member who retires this No- vember, and who will not pledge himself to support the free library movement, be contested, and let it be under- stood that the same course will he pursued at succeeding Novembers, if need be, and I think it will not be long be- fore we see the Library Cornm:ttee either re-moulded or stirred into action by the pressure of the Council. A RATEPAYER.

--- NATIONAL FOOTPATH PRE RVATION SOCIETY. Sir,—You sometime back kindly noticed this society, and perhaps you will oblige us with another few words in your paper on the progre:a we have made. There are now thirty-two vice-presidents, besides His Grace the Duke of Westminster, as patron, and the Earl of Becktive, president—our prospectus shows that upwards of forty members of the House of Commons (irrespective of party) have joined the society. We are constantly applied to from all parts of the country for advice respecting the closing of public footpaths and encroachments on roadside land, and I am glad to roport that three branch or local societies have lately been formed at Scarborough, Leicester, and Bristol—all doing excellent work. The Bristol society has already saved two footpaths. or I should say one was a country lane, which had boldly been taken possession of by a farmer and actually cultivated with wheat and potatoes! What audacity this, and yet there are some persona who ignorantly declare there is no necessity for such a Society. May I urge on the authorities in your locality to form a branch society to prevent illegal acts of this nature, or at all events they should mark the public footpaths red, on the 6 inch Ordnance Maps, hefore disputes arise. Parties desirous of erecting convenient stiles should obtain our Prospectus, which gives drawings of numerous stiles; it can be forwarded on receipt of two stamps. Our reporta are 63. each to non-members. An increase of members is much re- pired. I am, sir, yours very truly, HENRY ALLNUTT, Secretary.
42, EBsex-ereet, Strand.

THE WARRINGTON GERMAN CLASS. Sir,—l was much pleased to read the letter you pub. liehed a short time ago respecting the much desired move- ment set on foot by our respected townsman Mr. T. Morris. have Mt it a duty several times during the past year or two to draw your readers' attention to the steps taken in other manufacturing towns to push trade, and to the utter and complete blindness of our own manufacturers and workmen's societies to take similar steps. It has been more than once urged in the " Examiner " that the present action of competition, and the old routine system of conducting trade, do not work well together ; hence what is called "trade depression." That there is any lessening in producing powers is altogether out of the question. as anyone who cares to look into the facts rosy see for himself. Take either factory, forge, or mill, and compare the turn out with that of ten fifteen, or twenty years ago, and the reduction in cost, and increased amount of production, is simply amazing. Greater excellency in machinery at home has produced greater excellency abroad. As each firm seeks to eclipse its neighbour, so does one country seek to undersell and increase its production in its competitive struggle with another. I may be giving vent to an extreme pessimistic idea, but I am quite certain that we may look upon bad trade as the normal condition of things, to be relieved by occasional spurts, each spurt to be followed by a still more contracted state of trade, until not an eight hours' movement, but still fewer hours of labour, will be required to supply the wants

O f the world. In the meantime, and while the people are learning to fully appreciate the great socialistic revolution that is going on, we must live, and to do this we must make use of every method that offers itself. I suppose competition is some- thing like crime; once fairly in its embraces, and there 3 no knowing where it will leal us to; but of this be assured, it will find its level, and then, for them who live to see it,

Utopia. I have before me the two volumes issued by the Royal Commissioners on Technical Education. And here allow rue to say that these works, too expensive for workingmen to buy, are issued for the people, paid for by the people, and yet, only in rare cases do the people see them. In these volumes, information of the most important kind is con- veyed to the public, and if we are outdistanced in the struggle only ourselves will be to blame. A very clear moral is to be derived from the report, and one that em- ployers. as well as workmen, should lay well to heart, and that is, that the sooner Englishmen disabuse their minds as to their fancied superiority over other nations and the better for their pecuniary success. Large numbers of Eng- lish students are entered every year In continental schools, "leareing there the technical knowledge required, and "most alt the foreign students, on finishing their instruction, par- --lelcularly if they cannot enter a local factory on favourable "terms, tome to England for the purpose of completing their practical education in English factories, or with the hope of taking situations as designers or clerks." English manufacturers subscribe largely to the main. tenance of French schools, to have the benefit of sending English lads to learn designing. They also contribute largely to the local museums, of which no town is without. Leaving the reports and dealing with matters that come be- fore us every day, we find that Germans are exteneively employed in English houses. The London Chamber of Commerce, in a report issued on the subject, states that no fewer than 35 per cent. of the firms asked for information employ foreigners, whilst others employieg only English- men state that they will probably be obliged to break through their hitherto invariable, rule. Now, I ask English parents who are at their wits end what to do with their sons, what they think of this? Foreigners snpplantiny their own lads simply because there are so few public- spirited men like Mr. T. Morris The report says " the average German c.erk is better edncated than the average English clerk." He accepts a much smaller salary because Of the fact "that he considers his training in this country as a kind of apprenticeship or educational course." The German lad will leave home for France. When he has mastered the language thoroughly, he will coma with his double equipment to England, and when master of three languages and three methods of business, he is ready for any position. It is stated that our consuls and manufacturing represen- tatives are haying foreign agents introduced into their ranks. I copy the following from the "Ironmonger ": " The British Consular Corps counts in its ranks a great many agents who are of foreign nationality, and some who are at the head of large trade and ether establishments, who most be regarded as active competitors from the British point of view. In some other cages HIT Britannic Majesty's Consular agents are foreign bankers and foreign capitalists who hold a great many shares in works, the names of which are often known as active competitors of the English trader," From al this we can but corns to the conclusion that English employers, having made their "pile," are in. different to their workmen's case. In a series of Consular reports recently issued there is a loud cry for the increased employment in foreign countees of commercial travellers. This cry has been repeated again and again with emphasis. Our Consuls resident in Spain go so far as to say that unless British merchants send travellers competent as linguists, and Englishmen, they must be prepared to see the market pass into other hands. The German commercial traveller is everywhere. We send.' pamphlets, journale, circulars, and letters of in- quiry." and again I ask, why do we do this? The answer is: because our own youths are not thoroughly acquainted with the languages, and our travellers know nothing of the Manners, customs, and wants of the people. In Engtand, for a time, pending the Socialist era, it is necessary that our Trades Unions and other •workingmen societies should shake off old traditions, and clear them- selves from the shackles that undotibtadly are now holding the workers down. It is poseible for the Trades Court/oils of the country to inaugrate a new set of circumstances by lay- use themselves out for devoting their incomes to a great and national system of education. Workmen are the masters, and by wise combination could make our public scheole what they are not at present, places where their sons could be folly equipped for the battle of lyre. By taking these steps they would be masters of their own destinies, and would not need to be dependent, even on such clear- sighted friends as Mr. Thomas Morris. CLIFFORD DIX. P.S.-r-May I add that a summary of the report .of the Royal Commission on Technical Education has been issued by the Cobden Club. and may be heard of by applying to Mr. ll. Roberts, Liberal agent Bewsey-street. This is work Tories never do unless it be with the nation's money.

div.head: ANCIENT WINDOWS IN LYMM CHURCH.
div.p: ANCIENT WINDOWS IN LYMM CHURCH.

The following is from the Lymm Parish Maga- zine" for this month :—" We glean the following interesting facts from a paper read before the His- toric Society of Lancashire and Cheshire by Mr. J. P. Rylands, F.S.A. In most of the Cheshire, and many of the Lancashire churches, before the great rebellion, there -existed many very beautiful win- dows of painted glass, containing figures of the local gentry and their wives, with their shields of arms and monumental inscriptions. During the civil war of the great rebellion, the Puritans broke these windows and defaced the monuments. In the reign of Queen Elizabeth, in the years 1580 and 1592, one Thomas Chaloner took notes of the arms 'in the Lymm Church windows, and these notes, which consist of descriptions and rude drawings, I are preserved.iamong the Harleian Manuscripts in I the British Museum. The coats of arms described are those of the Warburtons, of Arley; of the family of Limme, of Lymm, anciently born by the West Hall branch of the Leghs, of High Legh ; of the Ctrosvenors, of Eaton, near Chester; of the family of Savage; of Hawarden, of Woolston, near W arrington ; of Hockenhull, of Prenton, in Wirral I Hundred. In describing the second of these coats I of arms, allusion is made to one Sir Thomas Dan- years, who distinguished himself at the battle of Crecy, in the year 1346, by relieving the standard of Edward the Black Prince when he was hard pressed by the enemy, and taking prisoner Count de Tankerville, chamberlain to the French King. The name Danyers we find later on corrupted into Daniels. This Sir Thomas Danyers lived at Bradley Hall, near Lymm. The present Bradley Hall is a farmhouse erected during the last fifty years, but is interesting, as it stands upon the site of the house to which Sir Thomas retired after the battle of Crecy, and where he probably died. The moat which still all but surrounds Bradley Hall is in a wonderful state of preservation."

ANNIVERSARY SERNIONS.—Two sermons were preached in the Union Church, Bridge-lane. Frodsham, on Sunday morning and evening, by the Rev J W Paull, MA., of Cheadle. Suitable hymns and anthems were sung br tbe choir, assisted by eeveral friends. The collections amounted to the sum of £l5 191 3d. Mwritonter Faun Cnnacrt.—On Sunday, two sermons were preached in the above chapel by the Rev W R Mullett, the newly-appointed circuit minister, and on Monday after- noon a public tea meettg was held in the schoolroom. A seception service was held afterwards, when Mr. White, of Helsby, presided, and addresses were given by the Revs E Hall, of Runcorn, and W R !gullet:, Mr T Shallcross, cir- cuit secretary, and ethers.
