E. A. ,Wright, Castle Park, Frodsham; William Hayes, Aehten ' Hayes, Chester; James Reynolds, Foxhill, Frodsham ; James Andrews, Frodsham ; Ralph Bate, Netherton ; L. Booth, Netherton ; William Booth (farmer). Frodsham ; I Henry Beewick. Barrow ; Thomas Davies, Frodsham •' John I.Dutton,Woodhouses ; Joseph Ellams, Helsby ; John Priest- ear, Frodsham ; James Percival. Godecroft ; Thomas Elias's, Helsby ; and William Garner, Netherton. REARING StIPPER.—A supper was given at the Bears Paw Hotel, Frodsham, on Siturday evening, to celebrate the erection of some stable buildings at Enfield, Frodsham, for the Misses Crosfiald. and also a coachman's cottage. The contractor for the stable and building is Mr. Thomas Davies and f*r the cottage, the executors of the late Mr. John Gleave. The architects for both buildings are Messrs. Linaker and Davies, of Frodsharn. The chair was taken by Mr. T. Davies, and he was supported by Mr. S. Davies, architect, Mr. George Gleave, and Mr. William Davies. Af- ter supper. the Chairman proposed the health of the Misses Crosfield, which was responded to by Mr. P. Davies, who also replied to the toast of "The architects." After several other toasts had been duly proposed and responded to the remainder of the evening was devoted to songs, the.. by the workmen, and a Very pleasant evening was spent. FAREWELL MEETING AND PRESENTATION.—OR Wednes- day evening a public meeting was held in the Triaity Wes- ' leyan school-roorn,Frodsham, for the purpose of bidding farewell to the Rev. E. and Mrs Mosscrop, and presenting a suitable testimonial to them prior to their leaving the Fred. sham circuit. Tnere was a good attendance. The Rev. F. F. Edmunds presided. Mr. Walter Robinson, the senior circuit steward, explained that the teachers of the Trinity Sunday school were the first to suggest a movement of this kind. He had to ask Mr. and Mrs Moescrop to accept the testimonials, which consisted of an unique stationery cabi- net and inkstand combined, a beautifully engraved silver tray and biscuit barrel. The inscription on the cabinetand tray read as follows Presented to the Rev. Edwin and Mrs Mosscrop by friends in the Frodsbam circuit, 31st August, 1887." Mr. Mosscrop, on behalf of Mrs Mosscrop and himself, bricfly thanked the friends for their kindness in presenting such valuable and handsome presents to them, and stated that during the past three years he had always endeavoured to do his duty under all circumstances, and that they bad never regretted coming to Frodsham to labour in the circuit. Mr. Bowdon, junior circuit stew- ard, together with Messrs Pickering, S. Walker. Proud, Limbert, P. Booth, and Captain Davies also addressed the meeting.

div.head: OUR FINANCIAL LETTER.
div.p: OUR FINANCIAL LETTER.

LFROM OUR OWN CORRESPONDENT.] 23, Old Broad-street, S.C. Apart from the fortnightly settlement which occupied the first three days of the week, there has been little doing on the Stock Exchange, although there has been some see-saw quotations, more especially in Americans. The holiday feeling still prevails. Capel Court and the public do not come to its relief. Another element in the consideration of the present state of the market is that there are few stocks on offer, as the bulk of the dividend earning stocks are held by bona fide investors, who do not rush on the market to take advantage of the "turn." • The half-yearly meeting cf the General Steam Navigation Company was held on Tuesday, and the general effect upon the shareholders was depressing. It is true the account shows an increase of earnings with a decrease of expendi- ture, but the chairman was bound to admit that toe traffic, returns were prejudicially affected by the competition of the Great Eastern Railway and the new Flushing route The chairman further cited the falling eff in the cattle trade as an item against them. Perhaps the most significant feature of the balance was the valuation of the company's vessels. This valuation works out at £l4 7s per registered ton. When we realize that on the best lines of ocean going steamers £l2 17s per ton is the highest estimate, it will be seen that there must be a serious deficiency. It is superfluous to remark that this formed the bone of contention at the meeting, but the shareholders seemed fully to realize that they could do nothing but hope for better things. A subject of censiderable comment in financial circles ; has been the registration of John Bright and Brothers RS a 'limited company. The capital of the company is £250,000, I divided into 1,420 ordinary shares of £lOO each. The ob- ject of the company is stated to be to purchase or otherwise acquire and carry on the business now carried on by MessrP. / John Bright and Brothers, as cotton spinners and manufac- turers and silk goods manufacturers, at Fieldhouse Mills, Rochdale, and also to carry on the business of Joian Bright and Co., carpet manufacturers, at the same place. The first subscribers are Mr. John Bright, M.P.. Mr. Thomas Bright, Mr. Jacob Bright, Mr. Frank John Bright, Mr. John Gilbert Bright, Mr. W. Leathern Bright, Mr. L. C. Bright, ' and P. Bright. The Right Honourable John Bright, Mr. I Thomas Bright, and Mr. Jacob Bright are to be directors of , the company during their lives or until they resign.

NONCMFORZIMS• IIND• 17113 CDlOlOlf. The Sectetary read the following letter :—" Greenway- ronst,Runcorn, Aumest 25th, 18t37. The Chairman of the Runcorn Improvement Commissioners. Dear sir,—At a meezing of the representatives of all the Nonconformist Sunliay schools, held in Brunswick Vestry, it was unani- mounly resolved That in view of the increasing diflicultV experienced in obtaining a suitable field for the scholars on Whit Nlbnday, the Improvement' Commissioners be requested to malos such alterations and'impromaments in the Common as will render it suitable for that purpose' I should be glad if you would bring this matter before the Board at your earliest convenience, and hoping they will accede to the reqcest,—l remain, vonrs-respecttelly, JoHN Boum), hon. secretary."—The Law Cferly remarked that the Board had not the power to spend a'penny on the Common. There was no other business, and the meeting ter- minated.

WIDNES SCHOOL BORRD The mo3thly m.eting waa held on Tueeday at the Town Hall. Mr. T.S. Timmis presided, and there were present the Rev. Dean Finegan, Rev. .7. Clarke, Ds. O'Keeffe, Messrs Bradshaw; Daacon, Imison, Wareing, and Daub'? (clerk).

DISTRICT EDUCATION. corsterirran. This Committee reported that during the month of July there were 257.person5 summonedbefore :the Committee for contravention of the Education Act, and 20 of these were prosecuted and convicted by the magistrates. There were 191 applications for school fees, which, were recommended to be paid in 170 cases.—Mr. Deacon proposed the adoption of the minutes —Dean Finegan seidthats he found that a great number of children attended school very irregularly, and at this season it was very importanta that the children should attend school. He had given Mt. Denby some names, and he hoped they would have the attention of the Corn- i mittee.—FaiherClarke said he had,given 49 names to Attendance Of'Acer Rowe, but he did ' not' know what had been the result.—Mr. Deacon replied thatethe committee ' thoroughly appreciated the difficulty a getting children to 1 reboot at present. Great difficulty was, experienced in getting the children to school because of' the measles, and many people took advantage of the prevalence of the disease to keep their children away, and it was- impossible to tell where measles existed and where they did not. There were, however, still measles in the town. At thnlost.meeting the committee had three or four certificates that certain chil- dren were not to be allowed to go to school he consequence of disease in the family. The committee- would do their ; beet to get the-children to school. CENSUS OF CHILDREa. The Education Committee also reported.. that during the holidays the attendance officers were empitoyed in taking a census of the children of the district, and several tables showing the results obtained were stibmittedi—Mr. Deacon, chairman of the committee, said the tables-showed that the number of housee-in Widnes was 5,112, am increase of 15 over two years ago, when the last census mem taken. The number of inhabited houses was 4924. being an increase of 214.. There were 188 houses and 39 tenses in course of erection. At' the last Census 12 houses were in course of erectione The number of children between three and 13 years was 7315 i an increase of 401. The number of school going c',lldren was 5,330, and the school+accommodation was 6,69s;,showhig an excess of accommodation of 1,368. Alluding to private schools, Mr. Deacon said it woe in his opinion matter for congratulation that there had been a de- crease of 91 in the number of childrens attending these schools, the totallnow being 112. A few years ago the Dis- trict Education Committee proposed a regulation with re- gard to these schools, and without injuring, them they had managed to decrease the number of childeen there. The number of children attending no school was 1,375, which was an increase of 100. The total number of: children over five who ought to be at school, but who were not, was 172. That number was larger than it ought to be ; but he had looked through' the various census returns himself, and be found,,with very few exceptions,- that the chil- dren were jest over five years of age. There were a few older children, but they were very. 2ew. One advan- tage of the ceneas was that these 172 childrent,were known, and he helieveet they were now on the roll& At all events on the SW May there were 6,278 children on the rolls, and last week there were 6,462 children on the rolls, which was an increase of 184. Showing that these children and a few others were on the rolls.. This was very satisfactory. The census showed that there was an increase of 554 children on the veils. The pro' portion of school-going children to the total population was as- one to 5-63. The population had been estirriated'at 30,000, but he did not knowewhether this num- ber was accurate or not. Taking the number of inhabited , houses at the census of 1881, and dividing that number in the populatioo, he believed there was an average of seven individbale to a house. If there was now a population of 30,000 j there were more people living in the same house than was the case in 1881. These figures seemed to point in that direction, but if there were anyi eases of overcrowd- ing it was for the Local Board te dret with.—The Chair- man observed that the average of the Ilnited Kingdom of school-going children to the population was Ito 6. He moved that the report be adopted, and that the committee be thanked for the great care they bad taken in the prepara- tion of the figures.—Mr. Bradshaw seconded the motion, 'which was carried unanimously. OVER-PRESSCRIA IN SCIWOLS.—TIOLAATION OF IDLES BY Treeceneese The School Management Committee reported that the following teachers had violated the circular letter, dated May 20th, 1886, viz. :—Messrs Snoddy and Showell, Missl Clayden, Mica Broad, Miss Strong, Miss Sampson, Mrs Chem, Miss Pornroy. and Misa Moege. The circular letter read as follows:—" I am desired by the School Manage- ment Committee to inform you that schoolrooms must be vacated at half-past four, and that the caretaker may enter any school at half-past four, except one room at the discre- tion of the head teacher of each department, which must be clear at five o'clock, except Friday, when it must be cleared at half-past five. I am, farther directed to say that all teachers must work strietly in accordance with their time table,. and any violation of these instructions will be considered by the committee as disobe- dience, and will be reported accordingly."—ln mov- ing the adoption of the. minutes, Dean Finegan said notwithstanding the instructions contained in the letter, several complaints had been made by parents. not only to the committee, but to ether members of the Board, about their children being detained in school after hours, and to a certain extent the complaints were correct. He did not come there to propose ante of censure upon the teachers, but he did say it was useless for the Board to make rules if those rules were to be violated. As chairman of the com- mittee he merely asked for instructions.—Father Clarke asked whose duty it was to see that these instructions-1 were carried out at the schools. Was it the duty of the. committee, or the clerk? It was absurd for the Board to. make rules for the teachers to do certain things if the Board was not going to insist upon the rules being observed.—The Chairman said the roles must be observed or they must be repealed. Suppose the teachers kept children in, was any report made of it ?---The Clerk : No, sir.—The Chairman 1, It can only be found out by complaints from the parents P he Clerk : Yes, sir.—Dean Finegan remarked that the last paragraph of the letter was the most important. The time table was sanctioned by Her Majesty's Inspecaor. and the Board in the strongest possible manner had intimated to the teachers that unless they worked up to that time table they should consider it a serious offence. After receiving complaints, he corresponded with Mr. Danby, who had made surprise visits and found the schools open at times when they should be closed.—The Chairman suggested that the clerk should write a strong letter to the teachers on the 1 matter.—Mr. Deacon : As one of those who had lent complaints to Dean Finegan on this mat- ter, he was very glad action had been taken, because there was no doubt that the irregularity had grown to large proportions in some schools It was to the credit of the teachers of one school that their names did did not appear on the list. There was another reason for stopping this Gvertime. There was no doubt that where a teacher kept the children in school three or four hours a week longer than another teacher he ought to get better results, if the Board judged the results simply by the per centage of pa.see. It was not fair to the teachers that had obeyed the Board's instructions.—Mr. Danby read a report of surprise visits he had made to the schools, showing that large numbers of children were kept in West Bank and Simm's Cross schools between four and five o'clock.—l was eventually decided that the teachers mentioned in th minute shouhl be writtcn to in strong terms by the clerk° the letters before being d.epat,hed to receive the approval, of Dean Finegan.

div.head: WOUNDING AFFRAY /F 1 RUNCORN.
div.p: WOUNDING AFFRAY /F 1 RUNCORN.

Yesterday, before Mr James Elandlry,at Honcorn Policer Court, Elizabeth Peacock was charged win unlawfully wounding Jane Drurv.—Drnry said she was a widow, and lived at 33, Back Cooper-street, with a man named John Ball. The prisoner lived in the next Muse with a man named Enoch Ditchaeld. On Monday night. the 15th Aug., she went to Ditchfield's house about sestin o'clock. and stood at the door talking with Ditchfield. Whilst she was standing there the prisoner ordered her away from the idoor. Ditchfteld told her to take no notice et!' the prisoner. Whereupon the prisoner took up a can which contained !beer from the table, and threw the liquor upon, Mrs. Green- way, who bad come upon the scene, and then threw the can at witness,. She avoided the can by stooping down.. Ditch• freld put the prisoner lute the front place, and'gave her a blow. The prisoner, however, again came to (ha kitchen door, and seizing her (witness) by the wrist pulled her Into the kitchen, and struck her on the back and arms with the p•ker. She (witness) screamed out for help,. and Mrs. Green way entered the mom, at the same time the prisoner struck her on the head with the poker, and she Ereame uncon,cious. She had lost a great Quantity of blood and bad been laid up ever since.— Mary An Crreenwav and Mary Ann Drury corroborated.— Dr. Nealow deposed that he bad attended the proseentrix, who bad suffered from a contused wound on the left side of the head,two inches in ferigth, above the ear. The wound was shaped :like the letter L., and penetrated to the bone. The wound required to be stitched. The woman waa now out of danger, but was very weak in cousequenci of the in- juries she had sustained. The poker produced was a very likely weapon to cease her injuries. P.C. Dutton deposed that when charged the prisoner said " I never did, so help me, God." OS the 23 d he took the prisoner to Knutsford, and during the journey she said '• I will give her more next time than. I have given her now. I will give her sornethingwortb going for."--The prisoner now alleged that the prosecutrix was the aggressor, and made her a black eye by striking her with a can.—She called Elizabeth Smithorho stated that the prosecutrix challenged the prisoner out to fight. The prisoner would not leave the house, and the prosecntrix entered and threw a bucket at her, and also struck her.—The prisoner was committed to the Quarter Sessions-for trial. The magistrate agreed to allow her eut on ball, herself in £2O, and two sureties of £lO each.

div.head: RUNCORN BoAar) OF COMMISSIONERS.
div.p: RUNCORN BoAar) OF COMMISSIONERS.

The monthly meeting was held at the Town Hall, on Wednesday. Mr Dobson presided, and there were present Messrs White, Fisher, Pritchard, Whittaker, Mellor, Taylor, Hankieson, Imisom and Grice with W. 11. Linaker (Law clerk) Marshall (Secretary), and Barker (Surveyor). The Highway and Buildings Committee submitted the following minute :—lt was recommended on the motion of Mr. Dobson seconded by Mr. Grioe that the application of the Runcorn Soap and Alkali Co. Limited, for permission to lay a pipe under the street from the Railway Station to the Old Soap. cry Works for conveying ammoniacal liquor from the station to each works be granted subject to an agreement that such pipes be laid at a lower depth than the gas and water mains and be laid to the satisfaction, and under the supervision of the Surveyor; and to a yearly acknowledgment of one ' guinea; the cost of such agreement to be borne by the ap- plicants.—Mr. Taylor' moved, and Mr. Hankinson seconded, the adoption of the minute.—Mr. Pritchard said while agreeing that it walethe duty of the Board to afford every 1 facility they could to the business of the town, he d ffered from the Committee as to charging a simple acknowledgment of I. in this ease. The sewers and gas and water Dines were laid free in the streets in accordance with Act of Par- liament because they were for the service and use of the general body of ratatpavers, but this application was from a private firm, who wished to use an important thoroughfare for trade purposes, and he thought it ought to be looked at purely as a business transaction. A simple acknowledg- ment should not satisfy the Hoard and they would be scarce- la; doing their duty to the ratepayers if they simply asked for an acknowledgment. He moved as an amendment that a charge of £s,be made, in consideration of the concession being made, on behalf of the ratepayers and the great facility that would be afforded to these works and also in considera- tion of the large saving in cartage. The saving io cartage might be £5O or considerably- more per annum and he thought the charge he named was only reasonable and the firm as business gentlemen would be prepared to pay it. Mr Grice said, at this time when they were expecting and hop- ing to see am improvement in the commerce of Runcorn and aa entire change in the position of the town, in conse- quence of the Manchester Ship .Canal, it would be unfortu- nate if it were to go forth to the manufacturers who might wish to settle in the town that, the Board of Commissioners were prepared to handicap them with irritating charges for conveniences to carry on their work. Instead of this con- cession being a disadvantage to the ratepayers, it would be a great advantage, because the Runcorn Soap and Alkali Company or any other firm in the town could put any number of horses and carts for the convenience of their works upon the roads, and putt the ratepayers to great ex- pense to keep the roads in order. The petting down of pipes would obviate this great expense to the Runcorn ratepayers. They had nothing to do with the savieg to the company, and it ought to go forth to the public that the Runcorn Commissioners had no intention of interfering with any- thing that would add to the progress of the town in the shape of neanufactories.—Mr. Pritchard said if horses end carts would have to use Lowlands-road to the great extent indicated by Mr. Grioe's assertions, the saving to the corn- pally would not merely be 250 as he had stated, but hun- dreds of pounds. Therefore he questioned whether the small charge he had mentioned was sufficient.—Mr. Prit- chard's amendment was not seconded, and the minute was adopted.

div.head: 'WEAVER TRUSTEFS.
div.p: THE 'WEAVER TRUSTEFS.

The Secretary read a letter from Mr. T. P. ungbes, general manager of the Weaver Trust, stating that Mr. W. Whittaker. one of the nominees of the Commissioners, had been appointed a member of the trust —Mr. W. H. Lin titer, clerk to the Runcorn Board of Guardians, wrote that the Guardians had unanimously passed the following resolu- tion ; 'That the clerk communicate with the following public bodies in the county of Chester, namely, Corporations, Improvement Commissioners, Local Boards, and Boards of Guardians, calling attention to the present self-elected repre- sentation on the Weaver Trust, with a view of devising some scheme by which the Weaver Trust shall be man- aged by a body of trustees elected by the rate- payers of the county." Mr. Linaker Raked the Commis- ' sinners to cooperate with the Guardians in the matter.— Mr. Grice moved that a reply should be sent to Mr. Una- ker that the Improvement Commissioners would co-operate with the Guardians of the Rencern Union in ascertaining the present position of the Weaver Trust, and if deemed advisable in moving to obtain the election of the trustees by the vote of the ratepayers. Mr. Taylor seconded the mo. I tion: They could do no harm by making this iniuiry, and if Caere was any advantage to the town to he derived they ought to have it.—Mr. Hankinson inquired if any expense would be entailed.—The Law Clerk said no. The work could be done by the Board's officials.—Mr. Itnison did not think there was any necessity to take steps in the matter at all. In a short time there would be a Govern- ment Bill that would regulate the actions of bodies of this kind, so that without any agitation from the Gnu- dians or the Commissioners the question would be righted by the Imperial Parliament. The Law Clerk said they would be no worse for having all the information at their finger ends, and it would cost nothing.—Mr.Grice intimated they would have to wait a very long time for the Local Government Mr. Pritchard said be should like to know what had oc- curred since two months ago, when gentlemen were nomi- nated to the Weaver Trust, that this question was moved In this manner. He did not think it was a fair or satisfactory mode of dealing with the matter to bring it up immediately after their representative, Mr. Whittaker, had been elected. —The Law Clerk was about to speak, when Mr. Pritchard said it did seem to be a helpless state for gentlemen to be in to have to appeal to the Law Clerk to hello them out of a difficulty. It was not a question of law.—Mr. Grine replied that he did not appeal to the Law Clerk for his assistance or his opinion. At the time Mr. Pritchard referred to this question was not before the Board. He had beard diesatis• faction expressed at the constitution of the Weaver Trust years ago, but the matter was not before the Board when Mr. Whittaker was elected. Mr. Whittaker was a gentleman respected by everyone in the town, and in taking upthismat- ter there was no feeling against Mr. Whittaker or any other gentleman. They were simply willing to co-operate with the Guardians in a matter which would be for the benefit of the county—The Law Clerk remarked that the Weaver Trust was a public trust belonging to the county, but it was managed by a body of self-elected truetees, meetings were held with closed doors and they only published an abstract of accounts which only occupied about 10 lines.— Mr. Taylor remarked that this question was brought before the Guardians months ago, and as it was now brought for- ward had nia reference to Mr. Whittaker.—The Law Clerk stated that last year the Weaver Trust earned about £6O 00e, and there was paid over to the county only about £15,030. —Mr. Pritchard moved that the Board take no action in the matter, and that a letter be sent to the Guardians stating the Commissioners would leave themselves perfectly open to receive any Information which the Guardians could offer

John Riley, of Elizabeth-street, and Michael Carr, of Oxford-street, young men of very rough appearance, were charged with having wounded Matthew Butler, a cooper, whose home is at 12, Ash-road. Immeuse quantities of rain fell, and the wind did considerable. damage to house property. A house in the Coventry-road was blown down, and the family had a iniraculons escape, a quan- tity of the &Apia; Jailing upon, a bed where a girl was . sleeping. The South Devon coast was. visited by a gale and heavy rain on Thursday night. The rivers have overflown, their banks. Great Damage has been done in the. Isle of Thanet and, Sandwich district of Kept to fruit, trees and hops by the. gale. A Monmouth telegram stAtes Thursday night a. severe gale, with a tremendous downpour of rain swept 07Ort that district. Roofs of houses and trees were much dam., aged, and the fruit crops suffered. A heavy sea is running in the Channel, and some ship. ping casualties are reported.. At Edinburgh, on Foiday, 'articles of fdrniture were loaf- ing about, and water reached the depth of 3f t. and 411. The lower pars of QueelfeLl'ark was also flooded to a depth of over 3ft. During the violent south-easterly gale at Portsmou* a large mission tent on, Southsea &lois:mon was blown away, and some of, the fumiture carried several hundred yPrds. Many small boats were smashed up on the beach.

div.head: ELECTION OF COMMISSIONERS AT RUNCORN.
div.p: ELECTION OF COMMISSIONERS AT RUNCORN.

The annual election ef five gentlemen to represent the ratepayers on the Board of Improvement Commissioners took place en Thursday. Of the retiring CommiseiOners four offered themselves for re-election, namely, Messrs. W. Whittaker, S. Taylor, F. A. Lake, and W. Fisher.. The fifth, Mr. W. Handley, who had not acted as a member of the Board since his election three years ago, did not again appeal for the suffrages of the townspeople. or this vacancy the issue practically lay between Mr, Joseph Williams, an old member of the Board, and Dir. Peter Smith, chemist. At the last contest Mr. Smithdailed to gain a seat on the Board bv one vote. He was than associa- ted with Mr. W. Hankinson, who was successful in being returned. but on the present occasion Mr. Sccetio, like Hal of the Wynd, fought for his own band, and he issued an independent address on Tuesday afternoon. He pointed out that neither religion nor politics entered into this con. test, and based his claim to represent the ratepayers upon his long residence amongst the ratepayers of Auncorn, and his intimate knowledge of the requirements of the town. He was, he added, more impressed than ever with the necessity for public baths, and i: elected he promised that he would use his utmost endeavours to introduce a scheme for the establishment of such an institution at amearly date. Mr. Smith also drew attention to the need of improvement to Waterloo Bridge, and avowed himself r.aronrable to an early settlement of the matter. The retiring members added ' the name of Mr. Joseph Williams, " an old and respected public servant," to their list, and asked the ratepayers to plump for the five gentlemen. No declaration of Dolicy was made on their behalf. Later, another placard WAS is- sued, in which Mr. Smith's name was associated with the retiring members, and upon this poster was the dealaration that the "works' Mid decided not ta take any active part in the election, a fact which left the result more oaen than would otherwise have been the ease. The poll was opened at eight o'clock at the Market Hall. Mr. James Dobson, the chairman of the Board of Commissioners, was the returning officer, and he was assisted in his duties by Mr. W. H. Linaker (the law clerk), Mr. E. Msrehall, (the secretary), and Mr. W. Sutton (the assist ant overseer).. There was a total absence of excitement throughout the whole of the day, most activity, being shown-by Mr. Smith's supporters. The poll was closed at four o'clock, and five minutes later Mr. Dobson declared the result as follows:--- P. Smith...39o W. VVhittaker...27o F, A. Lake 260 S. Tay10r...282 W. Fisher 261 J, Williams —lOl It may be stated as an interesting fact that only 359 per. sons voted, and the poll is. the lowest that has been recorded for a number of years, Mr. Smith was not present whert the result became known,, but a number of his supporters quickly brought him to, the spot, and he was loudly cheered. In, response to. calls for a speech, Mr. Smith returned thanks far having been place& at the head of the poll,and said ha. would use his utmost ea. deavoers to carry out the polity he had indicated in his address. (Cheers.) He was equally as strongly in favorer of baths that day as he was twelve montha ago, but he wished the public, distinctly to understand that he was not i going to make them a presont of bathe. (Hear, hear, and ' laughter.) They must remember that he waa only ono of a ' body of 18. gentlemen, an unless he had the support of a majority of the other Commissioners, he could not carry out his policy, but he, could assure them that he would stndy the interests of the ratepayers generally without fear or favour. (Cheers.) He concluded by pro- posing a note of thanks to the returning officer ler the admirable manner in which the election bad been conducted.— The motion was carried by anclamationi Mr, Dobson, in replyin, remarked that he 'braa

LAST NIGHT'S PARLIAMENT. HOUSE OF COMMONS, The House met at four o'clock. RAILWAY, TRAinezar.,nia4—Baron de wonswn replying to Mr. Addison,, said that ho fully recognised the importance of providing fer the protection of women trav'etling alone on railways. The Board oTrade had no statutory powers to interfere. A circular had been addressed to all the railway companies, asking that additional accommodation should be provided for women travelling alone and the Board believed that the companies would do all in their power to protect females travelling on their lines. SUPPLY.—The House vrent,inta Committee or Supply on. the Irish Civil Service Britimates.—On the vote for law charges and criminal prosectstions, Mr. CYRIL FLOWER complained that the recommendation of the committee that sat a year ago, that the Irieh Attorney General's salary should be reduced from £5,000 to £4,000., had not been car- ried out, whilst the recommendation to abolish the office of clerks to the Attorney-General, with a salary of £3OO per I annum, had been observed.—Mr. A. 1. BALFOUR said the salary of £5,000 was a great reduction on that which had formerly attached to the office, aedkcogsidering the res- ponsibility that rested on him, he thought the salary might not to be further redneed.—Mr T. IifEALY complained of the manner the law was administered in Ireland. He referred to a case that had recently occurred in Ireland, in which the police conatable who had been found guilty of wilful murder by the coroner's jury, was treated with the utmost leniency by the Crown officials, and who was 'never placed up to trial.—Mr. DEASY expressed similar opinions.—Mr. P. o'om:con said that which was termed justice in Ireland was nothing more than results brought about by juggling and fraud....-ATTORNRI-GENERAL for Ireland remied, and denied that the Government relied on packed juries and perjury evidence for convictions in crown prosecutions.— Mr. Clancy, Mr, J. The oecurence took place How changed was his manner from two days ago whilst the train was going between 30 and how changed from the wild grief and rapture of only 40 miles ti a hour. ten minutes ago, when he had forgotten everything but his love for Ilvacintli,—her utter devotion—her deadly peril. Now .his gaze, instead of boldly. seeking, almost shunned hers; he held her hand lightly ;he spoke as one who asks a favour. The woman he had haughtily claimed, despite her refusal of his suit, had saved his life,—had placed her honour, her name, in his habits. All the pure gold in the man's nature rose to the surface; all the dross was swept away ; he had wronged her ; , and she had heaped coals of fire on his head. - He turned and went out, and Hyacinth sank down on a low couch and covered her face, strangely happy; throngh all that made her anxious, for she was with Vincent Lorraine now. Whatever happened, she would be by his side; and her very presence at Curra- more would hasten the arrival of relief, for her mother, when she ascertained that her daughter had not been at Grady's farm to-night. would arrive at only one conclusion—that Lorraine had by some means taken her to tile castle; -and there would be not a moment lost in sending for aid to rescue her from her supposed imprisonment. Ali, if she could only hava spared her mother the anguish she must suffer ! but that could not, be. And her own name? Was it nothing to her that it might become a bye-word? Nay, no pure-hearted woman could think lightly of calumny that touches her fame ; yet stronger, higher emotions kept that fear in abeyance; and after all no one would misjudge her whose opinion she valued. Meanwhile Lorraine went down to Margaret, and bade her go out to the gatex warning her not even to open the little grille, but to call out that the master was absent, and no one could be admitted, his orders on that point being very strich Margaret—like most of her countrywomen—was very fearless; and, moreover, was in no darlger. She west out at once, ;aughing softly, for your Celt rarely fails to catch any touch of humour; and Lorraine, halting on the threshold of the postern, with his hand on his "six-shooter," heard her cry shrilly, as she reached the gate— " Who the divil are ye, ringing a place down an' an mild sowl out av her bed at thisehne ?" , " Ocir!" rAurned a childish voice in well simulated agitation—" I must see the masther ; for the,-love o' the Vargin, let me in !" "'What's the matther ? Misther Lorraine isn't at hpme, nor won't be till the early maiming. What have ye got to tell hint, ye little screcchin't aptdpeen?":' "'What I'll tell to his ear alone, mistliress ; an' if' he's out, Mix, I'll wait for him; but och ! the thun- dher's comin' ; let me in. • I couldn't harm ye if I would." "Let ye in? Its more than I'd dare—the mother's' so shtrict; else I'd be willin'. Ye must get shilter where ye can if ye won't give yer message to me." And back trotted old Margaret, and re-entered the kitchen, chuckling, and Lorraine closed and barred up the postern. " They are booked till the morning, Margaret," he said, quietly. "Go and lie down now, and take some rest." "Shore, yer anner, Miss Hyacinth will want some- thin' to ate. Och ! 'tis the nolilest girl that leer drew breath. Forgive me that I say it, yer anner, but Uri glad I am to see ye love her, 'an share she'll be no woman that doesn't love you." The Mood rushed to Lorraine's brow,. . "Forgive you?" he, said, in a low voice. "I see nothing to forgive, Margaret. But I will see to Miss Hyacinth. I will not hesitate to call you if I need you." "Very well. thank yer anner—l'll jest lie down in the room yonder, an' then I'll be handy." And Lorraine turned back to the room where he had left Hyacinth.
